questions.stem: Which part of an animal cell controls the cell's activities and contains the genetic material?
options: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Cytoplasm
Mitochondria
questions.hint: Think of the cell's "control centre".
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — It holds the chromosomes (DNA), which carry the instructions for everything the cell does.
B: Incorrect — This controls what goes in and out of the cell, not the cell's activities.
C: Incorrect — This is the jelly where most chemical reactions happen. It doesn't hold the genetic material.
D: Incorrect — These release energy by aerobic respiration. They don't control the cell.

questions.stem: In which part of a cell does aerobic respiration take place?
options: Ribosomes
Mitochondria
Cell wall
Nucleus
questions.hint: This part is often called the "powerhouse" of the cell.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. They don't carry out respiration.
B: Correct — Aerobic respiration happens here, releasing energy for the cell.
C: Incorrect — The cell wall strengthens plant cells. No reactions for energy happen there.
D: Incorrect — The nucleus holds the genetic material and controls the cell.

questions.stem: What is the function of ribosomes?
options: Storing cell sap
Photosynthesis
Protein synthesis (making proteins)
Controlling what enters and leaves the cell
questions.hint: They are tiny, and found in every type of cell, even bacteria.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cell sap is stored in the permanent vacuole of plant cells.
B: Incorrect — Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts.
C: Correct — Ribosomes join amino acids together to build proteins.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of the cell membrane.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
options: Mitochondria
Chloroplast
Nucleus
Cell membrane
questions.hint: Which part captures light?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells respire, so both have mitochondria.
B: Correct — Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis. Animal cells don't photosynthesise, so they don't have them.
C: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus.
D: Incorrect — Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane.

questions.stem: What is the cell wall of a plant cell made of?
options: Starch
Cellulose
Glucose
Protein
questions.hint: It is a tough carbohydrate that makes up plant fibres.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Starch is a carbohydrate plants use to store energy, not to build cell walls.
B: Correct — Cellulose fibres make the cell wall strong, which supports the cell.
C: Incorrect — Glucose is a sugar made in photosynthesis. Plants turn some of it into cellulose, but the wall itself is cellulose.
D: Incorrect — Plant cell walls aren't made of protein.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium?
options: It is much larger than a eukaryotic cell
It contains chloroplasts
Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus
It has a nucleus and mitochondria
questions.hint: "Pro" cells are simpler than eukaryotic cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Prokaryotic cells are much smaller, roughly 10 to 100 times.
B: Incorrect — Bacteria don't have chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are found in plant cells.
C: Correct — Bacteria have a single loop of DNA floating in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called plasmids.
D: Incorrect — These are features of eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi).

questions.stem: What are plasmids?
options: Rings of DNA inside the nucleus of plant cells
Organelles that release energy in plant cells
Structures that make proteins
Small rings of DNA found in bacteria
questions.hint: They are extra DNA found in bacteria.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bacteria don't have a nucleus, and plasmids aren't found in plant nuclei.
B: Incorrect — That describes mitochondria.
C: Incorrect — That is what ribosomes do.
D: Correct — Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells.

questions.stem: A bacterium is 2 µm long. An animal cell is 20 µm across. How many times bigger is the animal cell?
options: 100 times
10 times
18 times
40 times
questions.hint: Divide the bigger size by the smaller size.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would need the animal cell to be 200 µm.
B: Correct — 20 ÷ 2 = 10. That is one order of magnitude bigger.
C: Incorrect — 18 is the difference (20 − 2). "How many times bigger" means divide, not subtract.
D: Incorrect — 40 is 20 × 2. You need to divide, not multiply.

questions.stem: Why does a sperm cell contain lots of mitochondria?
options: To release energy for the tail to swim
To give the cell a strong wall
To make food by photosynthesis
To store the father's genetic material
questions.hint: What does a sperm cell need to do to reach the egg?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases the energy the tail needs to move.
B: Incorrect — Mitochondria don't make walls, and animal cells have no cell wall.
C: Incorrect — Sperm cells are animal cells and can't photosynthesise.
D: Incorrect — The genetic material is in the nucleus in the head of the sperm.

questions.stem: How is a root hair cell adapted to its job?
options: It has many ribosomes to digest the soil
It has a very thick cell wall to protect it from soil
It has many chloroplasts to photosynthesise underground
It has a long projection that gives a large surface area
questions.hint: Its job is absorbing water and minerals from the soil.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. Root hair cells don't digest soil.
B: Incorrect — A thick wall would slow down absorption. That is the opposite of what it needs.
C: Incorrect — There is no light underground, so root hair cells have no chloroplasts.
D: Correct — More surface touching the soil means water and mineral ions are absorbed faster.

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a cell's image is 6 mm wide. The real cell is 0.02 mm wide. What is the magnification?
questions.hint: Magnification = image size ÷ real size.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
B: Incorrect — Too big by 10 times. Check the decimal place: 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
C: Incorrect — Check the division: 6 ÷ 0.02 = 300.
D: Incorrect — This multiplies the two sizes. You need image size ÷ real size.

questions.stem: Why can scientists see ribosomes with an electron microscope but not with a light microscope?
options: Electron microscopes have a much higher magnification and resolution
Electron microscopes show cells in colour
Electron microscopes can look at living cells
Ribosomes only exist in cells prepared for electron microscopes
questions.hint: Think about how much detail each microscope can show.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Higher resolution means two points very close together can be seen as separate, so tiny structures like ribosomes become visible.
B: Incorrect — Electron microscope images are black and white. Colour is added afterwards.
C: Incorrect — The specimens must be dead. This is a disadvantage of electron microscopes.
D: Incorrect — Ribosomes are in all cells. They are just too small for a light microscope to show.

questions.stem: A light microscope has a magnification of × 400. The image of a cell is 10 mm long. What is the real length of the cell?
options: 4 µm
250 µm
2.5 µm
25 µm
questions.hint: Real size = image size ÷ magnification. Then convert mm to µm (1 mm = 1000 µm).
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This divides the magnification by the image size (400 ÷ 10 ÷ 10). The formula is image ÷ magnification.
B: Incorrect — Too big by 10 times. 10 ÷ 400 = 0.025 mm = 25 µm.
C: Incorrect — The decimal place has slipped. 0.025 mm is 25 µm, not 2.5 µm.
D: Correct — 10 ÷ 400 = 0.025 mm. 0.025 × 1000 = 25 µm.

questions.stem: Which statement about cell differentiation is correct?
options: Differentiated cells can easily change into any other type of cell
Most plant cells differentiate early on, but many animal cells can differentiate throughout life
Most animal cells differentiate early on, but many plant cells can differentiate throughout life
Animal and plant cells both stop differentiating at birth
questions.hint: Think about which can regrow from a cutting: a plant or a person?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Once a cell has specialised, it usually can't change into another type.
B: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
C: Correct — That is why you can grow a whole new plant from a cutting, but an adult human can't regrow a lost arm.
D: Incorrect — Plants keep growing new specialised cells at their meristems all their lives.

questions.stem: In school labs, bacteria cultures are usually incubated at a maximum of 25 °C. Why?
options: To kill any bacteria that might be harmful
To reduce the chance of growing bacteria that could cause disease in humans
Because 25 °C is the temperature at which all bacteria grow fastest
Because the agar jelly melts above 25 °C
questions.hint: Which bacteria grow best at human body temperature?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 25 °C doesn't kill bacteria. It is a warm temperature where many bacteria can still grow.
B: Correct — Human pathogens grow best near body temperature (37 °C). Keeping it at 25 °C makes them much less likely to grow.
C: Incorrect — Many bacteria grow faster at higher temperatures. 25 °C is chosen for safety.
D: Incorrect — Agar stays solid well above 37 °C. It only melts at very high temperatures.

questions.stem: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, how many will there be after 2 hours?
questions.hint: Work out how many times it divides, then double that many times.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — 2 hours = 120 minutes. 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. 2⁶ = 64.
B: Incorrect — This doubles the number of divisions (6 × 2). The population doubles each time, so it's 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.
C: Incorrect — 32 is 2⁵, which is only 5 divisions. 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions.
D: Incorrect — 6 is the number of divisions, not the number of bacteria.

questions.stem: Where are chromosomes found in an animal cell?
options: In the cell membrane
In the cytoplasm
In the nucleus
In the ribosomes
questions.hint: They carry the genetic material.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The membrane controls what enters and leaves. It doesn't hold chromosomes.
B: Incorrect — In animal cells, chromosomes are kept inside the nucleus, not loose in the cytoplasm.
C: Correct — Chromosomes are found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
D: Incorrect — Ribosomes make proteins. They don't contain chromosomes.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.hint: Chromosomes come in pairs, and humans have 23 pairs.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 92 would be double the normal number.
B: Correct — 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes.
C: Incorrect — 44 is two short. Don't forget the pair of sex chromosomes.
D: Incorrect — 23 is the number of pairs. Sex cells (eggs and sperm) have 23, but body cells have 46.

questions.stem: What is a chromosome made of?
options: Cell membrane
Glucose and starch
A DNA molecule that carries many genes
A single gene
questions.hint: It is a long, coiled molecule that carries genes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The membrane surrounds the cell. It isn't part of a chromosome.
B: Incorrect — These are carbohydrates. They don't carry genetic information.
C: Correct — Each chromosome is one long DNA molecule with a large number of genes along it.
D: Incorrect — A chromosome carries many genes, not just one.

questions.stem: What does mitosis produce?
options: Four genetically different cells
Two genetically different cells
One larger cell
Two genetically identical cells
questions.hint: Mitosis is used for growth and repair, so the new cells must be copies.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes meiosis, which makes sex cells.
B: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical cells, not different ones.
C: Incorrect — Mitosis splits one cell into two. It doesn't join cells together.
D: Correct — Mitosis makes two daughter cells with exactly the same chromosomes as the parent cell.

questions.stem: What happens in the first stage of the cell cycle, before mitosis?
options: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide
The cell joins with another cell
One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
The cell grows, copies its DNA and makes more ribosomes and mitochondria
questions.hint: The cell gets ready to split into two.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is the final stage, which forms two cells.
B: Incorrect — Cells don't join together in the cell cycle.
C: Incorrect — This happens during mitosis, the second stage.
D: Correct — The cell needs two full sets of everything, one for each new cell.

questions.stem: Why is cell division by mitosis important in multicellular organisms?
options: To make sex cells (gametes)
To create genetic variation
To release energy from glucose
For growth and repair
questions.hint: What happens when you cut your skin?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gametes are made by meiosis, not mitosis.
B: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical cells, so it doesn't create variation.
C: Incorrect — That is respiration, not cell division.
D: Correct — Mitosis makes new identical cells, so the body can grow and replace damaged cells.

questions.stem: During mitosis, what happens to the chromosomes?
options: The chromosomes are destroyed
The number of chromosomes is halved
One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
The chromosomes join with chromosomes from another cell
questions.hint: Each new cell needs a full set.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The chromosomes are kept. The new cells need them.
B: Incorrect — Halving happens in meiosis, not mitosis.
C: Correct — So each new cell gets a full, identical set of chromosomes.
D: Incorrect — That happens at fertilisation, not mitosis.

questions.stem: What happens in the final stage of the cell cycle?
options: The cell grows bigger
The DNA is copied
The cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells
Chromosomes are pulled to each end of the cell
questions.hint: This stage finishes the split.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Growth happens in the first stage.
B: Incorrect — DNA is copied in the first stage, before mitosis.
C: Correct — This completes the cell cycle.
D: Incorrect — This is mitosis, the stage before.

questions.stem: What is a stem cell?
options: A specialised cell found only in plant stems
A cell that has lost its nucleus
A cell that can only make more cells of exactly its own type
An undifferentiated cell that can make more cells and turn into other types of cell
questions.hint: It hasn't "chosen a job" yet.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stem cells are found in animals and plants. The name has nothing to do with plant stems.
B: Incorrect — Stem cells have a nucleus. They need their DNA to divide.
C: Incorrect — Stem cells can differentiate into other types too.
D: Correct — Stem cells aren't specialised yet, so they can divide and become different cell types.

questions.stem: Where are stem cells found in plants?
options: Xylem
Meristems
Guard cells
Root hair cells
questions.hint: These areas are at the tips of roots and shoots, where the plant grows.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Xylem is specialised tissue that carries water.
B: Correct — Meristem tissue can differentiate into any type of plant cell, all through the plant's life.
C: Incorrect — Guard cells are specialised to open and close stomata.
D: Incorrect — Root hair cells are already specialised to absorb water.

questions.stem: How do embryonic stem cells differ from adult bone marrow stem cells?
options: There is no difference between them
Embryonic stem cells can't divide
Adult bone marrow stem cells can turn into any type of cell; embryonic ones can't
Embryonic stem cells can turn into most types of human cell; adult bone marrow stem cells can only form some types, such as blood cells
questions.hint: Which is younger and less specialised?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Embryonic stem cells can form many more types of cell.
B: Incorrect — Embryonic stem cells divide very easily.
C: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
D: Correct — That is why embryonic stem cells could be used to treat more conditions.

questions.stem: In therapeutic cloning, an embryo is made with the same genes as the patient. Why is this useful?
options: Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body
It can cure every genetic disease
It means there are no ethical objections
The stem cells grow faster than normal cells
questions.hint: Think about what the immune system does to cells it doesn't recognise.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The cells have the patient's own genes, so the immune system treats them as "self".
B: Incorrect — It isn't a cure for everything. Research is still going on.
C: Incorrect — Many people still object, because an embryo is used and then destroyed.
D: Incorrect — Matching genes is about avoiding rejection, not speed.

questions.stem: Which is a risk of using stem cells in medical treatment?
options: Transfer of a viral infection to the patient
The stem cells always cause the patient to die
The stem cells can't divide once inside the patient
The patient's DNA is permanently changed into the donor's
questions.hint: Cells grown in a lab could carry something harmful.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — If the stem cells are infected with a virus, the patient could catch it.
B: Incorrect — This is not true. Bone marrow transplants already save lives.
C: Incorrect — The worry is more about cells dividing out of control, not failing to divide.
D: Incorrect — A treatment doesn't replace all of the patient's DNA.

questions.stem: A human body cell (46 chromosomes) divides by mitosis, and then both new cells divide by mitosis again. How many cells are there, and how many chromosomes does each have?
options: 2 cells, each with 46 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 92 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 23 chromosomes
4 cells, each with 46 chromosomes
questions.hint: Mitosis doubles the number of cells but keeps the chromosome number the same.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is after only one division. There were two rounds.
B: Incorrect — DNA is copied before division, but each new cell still ends up with 46.
C: Incorrect — Halving to 23 only happens in meiosis.
D: Correct — 1 → 2 → 4 cells. Mitosis keeps the full set of 46 in every cell.

questions.stem: Why do plant growers use meristem tissue to make clones?
options: To make large numbers of identical plants with useful features quickly and cheaply
To increase genetic variation in the crop
To make plants that don't need light
Because meristem cells can't divide
questions.hint: Think about speed and getting exactly the plant you want.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — For example, disease-resistant crops, or saving rare species from extinction.
B: Incorrect — Clones are identical, so there is no variation. That is actually a risk if a new disease appears.
C: Incorrect — Cloned plants still need light for photosynthesis.
D: Incorrect — Meristem cells divide very easily. That is why they are used.

questions.stem: What is diffusion?
options: The movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of particles from a lower concentration to a higher concentration
The movement of particles using energy from respiration
The net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration
questions.hint: Particles spread out from where there are lots of them.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes osmosis, a special type of diffusion.
B: Incorrect — That is active transport, which needs energy.
C: Incorrect — Diffusion is passive. It doesn't need energy.
D: Correct — Particles spread out down a concentration gradient. No energy is needed.

questions.stem: Which gas diffuses from the air in the lungs into the blood?
options: Nitrogen
Water vapour
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
questions.hint: Your cells need this gas for aerobic respiration.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Nitrogen isn't taken up by the body. It's breathed out unchanged.
B: Incorrect — Water vapour is breathed out, not absorbed for respiration.
C: Correct — There is more oxygen in the air in the lungs than in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood.
D: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, from the blood into the lungs, to be breathed out.

questions.stem: What is osmosis?
options: The movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of water from a concentrated solution to a more dilute solution
The movement of salt particles across a membrane
The movement of water using energy from respiration
questions.hint: It is only about water.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Water moves to where there is less water, and more solute.
B: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
C: Incorrect — Osmosis is the movement of water, not solutes.
D: Incorrect — Osmosis is passive. It doesn't need energy.

questions.stem: What does active transport need that diffusion does not?
options: Sunlight
Energy from respiration
Nothing, they are the same process
Water
questions.hint: It moves substances "uphill".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sunlight is needed for photosynthesis, not active transport.
B: Correct — Moving substances against a concentration gradient takes energy.
C: Incorrect — They are different. Diffusion goes down a gradient for free; active transport goes up it using energy.
D: Incorrect — Active transport moves dissolved substances, but water isn't what makes it different from diffusion.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
options: A smaller surface area
A bigger difference in concentration
A thicker membrane
A lower temperature
questions.hint: Think: difference in concentration, temperature, surface area.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Less surface means fewer particles can cross at once.
B: Correct — A steeper concentration gradient means faster diffusion.
C: Incorrect — Particles have further to travel, so diffusion is slower.
D: Incorrect — Particles move more slowly when it's colder, so diffusion slows down.

questions.stem: Urea is a waste product made in cells. Where does it diffuse to?
options: From the blood into the cells
From the cells into the stomach
From the cells into the blood plasma, to be removed by the kidneys
From the cells into the lungs to be breathed out
questions.hint: It needs to get to the kidneys.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the wrong way. Cells make urea, so their concentration is higher.
B: Incorrect — Urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys, not the stomach.
C: Correct — There is more urea in the cells than in the plasma, so it diffuses into the blood.
D: Incorrect — Urea is removed in urine, not breathed out.

questions.stem: Root hair cells take in mineral ions by active transport. Why can't they use diffusion?
options: Root hair cells don't have a cell membrane
The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is usually lower than inside the root
Mineral ions are too big to move at all
The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is usually higher than inside the root
questions.hint: Compare the amount of minerals in the soil with the amount inside the root.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — All cells have a cell membrane.
B: Correct — To move ions from low to high concentration, the cell must use energy.
C: Incorrect — They do move. They just need energy to go against the gradient.
D: Incorrect — If that were true, diffusion would work. The soil is usually more dilute.

questions.stem: After a meal, sugar is absorbed from the gut into the blood even when the blood has more sugar than the gut. How?
options: By diffusion
By osmosis
By photosynthesis
By active transport
questions.hint: Moving against a gradient needs energy.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Diffusion can only move sugar from a higher to a lower concentration.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis only moves water.
C: Incorrect — Photosynthesis is how plants make glucose. It doesn't move it.
D: Correct — Active transport uses energy from respiration to move sugar into the blood against the concentration gradient.

questions.stem: A piece of potato is left in a very concentrated salt solution. What happens to its mass?
options: It decreases, because water leaves the potato cells by osmosis
It increases, because salt enters the potato by osmosis
It increases, because water enters the potato cells by osmosis
It stays the same, because potatoes don't do osmosis
questions.hint: Which side has more water, the potato cells or the salty solution?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The solution is more concentrated, so water moves out of the cells.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt.
C: Incorrect — Water would enter if the solution were more dilute than the cells, like pure water.
D: Incorrect — Potato cells have partially permeable membranes, so osmosis happens.

questions.stem: Why doesn't a single-celled organism, like an amoeba, need special exchange surfaces?
options: It has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion through its membrane is fast enough
It doesn't need oxygen or food
It uses osmosis to get oxygen
It has a small surface area to volume ratio
questions.hint: Think about surface area compared with volume.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Substances only have a short distance to travel, so diffusion meets its needs.
B: Incorrect — All living organisms need to exchange substances.
C: Incorrect — Osmosis only moves water. Oxygen enters by diffusion.
D: Incorrect — Small organisms have a large ratio, not a small one.

questions.stem: A 1 cm cube has a surface area to volume ratio of 6 : 1. What is the ratio for a 2 cm cube?
questions.hint: Surface area = 6 × (side × side). Volume = side × side × side.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³. 24 : 8 = 3 : 1.
B: Incorrect — The ratio changes as the cube gets bigger. Bigger objects have a smaller ratio.
C: Incorrect — This is upside down. The ratio is surface area : volume = 24 : 8.
D: Incorrect — The ratio gets smaller as the cube gets bigger, not larger.

questions.stem: In the osmosis practical, a potato cylinder goes from 2.00 g to 2.30 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
questions.hint: % change = (change ÷ starting mass) × 100.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This divides by the final mass (2.30). Always divide by the starting mass.
B: Incorrect — The mass went up, so the change is positive.
C: Correct — Change = 0.30 g. 0.30 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = 15%. It gained mass, so it's +15%.
D: Incorrect — This uses 0.30 as if it were the percentage. You must divide by the starting mass.

questions.stem: In the osmosis practical, potato pieces in 0.3 mol/dm³ sugar solution don't change mass. What does this tell you?
options: No water molecules move at all
The potato cells are dead
The solution inside the potato cells has about the same concentration as 0.3 mol/dm³
The sugar has entered the potato cells
questions.hint: No change in mass means no net movement of water.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Water still moves both ways. It just balances out.
B: Incorrect — Osmosis happens across the membrane whether or not the result shows a change.
C: Correct — Water moves in and out at the same rate, so there is no net movement.
D: Incorrect — The cell membrane stops sugar moving in this practical. Only water moves.

questions.stem: Which feature would make an exchange surface, like the lungs or fish gills, LESS effective?
options: A large surface area
A thick lining
Being ventilated
A good blood supply
questions.hint: Good exchange surfaces are big, thin and well supplied with blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A large surface area makes exchange faster.
B: Correct — A thick lining increases the distance particles must travel, so diffusion is slower.
C: Incorrect — Ventilation brings in fresh air or water, keeping the gradient steep.
D: Incorrect — Blood carries substances away, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

questions.stem: A red blood cell and a plant cell are both put in pure water. The red blood cell bursts but the plant cell doesn't. Why?
options: Plant cells don't take in water by osmosis
Water leaves the red blood cell, making it burst
The red blood cell has a cell wall that splits
Water enters both cells by osmosis, but the plant cell has a cell wall that stops it bursting
questions.hint: Which cell has extra support around it?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They do, which is why the plant cell swells and becomes firm.
B: Incorrect — Water enters the red blood cell. Losing water would make it shrink.
C: Incorrect — Animal cells, including red blood cells, have no cell wall.
D: Correct — The strong cellulose wall pushes back, so the plant cell just becomes firm (turgid).

questions.stem: What is a tissue?
options: A single cell that carries out one job
A group of different tissues doing a specific job
A group of organs working together
A group of cells with a similar structure and function
questions.hint: Think of what the cells in a tissue have in common.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A tissue is made of many cells, not just one.
B: Incorrect — That describes an organ.
C: Incorrect — That describes an organ system, not a tissue.
D: Correct — The cells in a tissue are alike and work together to do one job, e.g. muscle tissue contracts.

questions.stem: Which list is in the correct order, from smallest to largest?
options: Tissue → cell → organ → organ system → organism
Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
Organism → organ system → organ → tissue → cell
questions.hint: Start with the basic building block of all living things.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Tissues are made of cells, so cells must come first.
B: Correct — Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems make up the organism.
C: Incorrect — Organs are made of tissues, so tissue must come before organ.
D: Incorrect — This is the right sequence but backwards: it goes from largest to smallest.

questions.stem: Which of these is an organ?
options: A red blood cell
Muscle tissue
The digestive system
The stomach
questions.hint: An organ is made of several different tissues working together.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is a single cell, not an organ.
B: Incorrect — This is one tissue. An organ is made of several tissues.
C: Incorrect — This is an organ system: a group of organs working together.
D: Correct — The stomach contains muscle, glandular and epithelial tissue working together to digest food.

questions.stem: What is an organ system?
options: A group of cells with a similar structure
All the cells of one type in the body
A group of organs that work together to do a particular job
A group of tissues inside one organ
questions.hint: It is the level just below the whole organism.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes a tissue.
B: Incorrect — Cells of one type working together form a tissue, not an organ system.
C: Correct — For example, the digestive system includes the stomach, small intestine, liver and pancreas.
D: Incorrect — That describes an organ, not an organ system.

questions.stem: What are the basic building blocks of all living organisms?
options: Cells
Atoms
Tissues
Organs
questions.hint: Every living thing, from bacteria to whales, is made of these.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — All living things are made of one or more cells.
B: Incorrect — Everything is made of atoms, living or not. In biology, the basic unit of life is the cell.
C: Incorrect — Tissues are made of cells, and single-celled organisms have no tissues at all.
D: Incorrect — Organs are made of tissues, which are made of cells.

questions.stem: Which of these is a tissue rather than an organ?
options: The pancreas
A leaf
Glandular tissue
The heart
questions.hint: Is it made of one type of cell, or several types of tissue?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The pancreas is an organ made of several tissues, including glandular tissue.
B: Incorrect — A leaf is a plant organ made of epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem tissues.
C: Correct — Glandular tissue is a group of similar cells that make and release substances such as enzymes.
D: Incorrect — The heart is an organ made of muscle, nervous and connective tissue.

questions.stem: A leaf contains epidermal tissue, mesophyll tissue, xylem and phloem. What does this tell you about a leaf?
options: It is a single specialised cell
It is a tissue, because all its cells are plant cells
It is an organ system, because it has more than one tissue
It is an organ, because it is made of several tissues working together
questions.hint: Count how many types of tissue are working together.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A leaf is made of millions of cells of different types.
B: Incorrect — Being plant cells isn't enough. A tissue is one group of similar cells.
C: Incorrect — An organ system is made of several organs, not several tissues.
D: Correct — Several tissues working together to carry out a function (photosynthesis) is what makes an organ.

questions.stem: In the stomach, which tissue churns the food and contents around?
options: Xylem tissue
Epithelial tissue
Muscular tissue
Glandular tissue
questions.hint: Which tissue can contract?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Xylem is a plant tissue, not found in animals.
B: Incorrect — Epithelial tissue covers the inside and outside of the stomach.
C: Correct — Muscular tissue contracts to churn the food and mix it with digestive juices.
D: Incorrect — Glandular tissue makes digestive juices. It doesn't move the food.

questions.stem: In the stomach, what is the job of glandular tissue?
options: To churn the food
To cover the outside and inside of the stomach
To absorb digested food into the blood
To produce digestive juices, such as enzymes and acid
questions.hint: Glands release (secrete) substances.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the job of the muscular tissue.
B: Incorrect — That is the job of the epithelial tissue.
C: Incorrect — Most absorption happens in the small intestine, not the stomach.
D: Correct — Glandular tissue secretes juices containing protease enzymes and hydrochloric acid.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches an organ to the organ system it belongs to?
options: Heart: digestive system
Lungs: digestive system
Small intestine: digestive system
Stomach: circulatory system
questions.hint: Think about what each organ actually does.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The heart pumps blood. It belongs to the circulatory system.
B: Incorrect — The lungs exchange gases. They belong to the breathing (respiratory) system.
C: Correct — The small intestine digests and absorbs food, so it is part of the digestive system.
D: Incorrect — The stomach digests food. It belongs to the digestive system.

questions.stem: Which organ systems work together to get oxygen from the air to a muscle cell in your leg?
options: The breathing (respiratory) system and the circulatory system
The breathing system only
The digestive system and the nervous system
The digestive system and the circulatory system
questions.hint: One system takes oxygen in; another moves it around the body.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The lungs take in oxygen, then the heart and blood vessels carry it to the cells.
B: Incorrect — The lungs take in oxygen, but without the blood it couldn't reach your leg.
C: Incorrect — Neither of these takes in or carries oxygen.
D: Incorrect — The circulatory system carries oxygen, but the digestive system takes in food, not oxygen.

questions.stem: A cell is about 0.01 mm across and an organ is about 10 cm long. Roughly how many times bigger is the organ than the cell?
options: 100 times
1 000 000 times
10 000 times
1000 times
questions.hint: Change both lengths to the same unit first. 1 cm = 10 mm.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is too small. Change 10 cm into mm, then divide by 0.01.
B: Incorrect — This is too big. 100 mm ÷ 0.01 mm = 10 000.
C: Correct — 10 cm = 100 mm, and 100 ÷ 0.01 = 10 000.
D: Incorrect — Check your units: 10 cm is 100 mm, not 10 mm.

questions.stem: Why do large multicellular organisms like humans need organ systems, when a single-celled organism does not?
options: Diffusion doesn't happen in large organisms
Their cells don't need oxygen or food
Their cells are too far from the outside for substances to reach them quickly by diffusion alone
Their cells are bigger than the cells of single-celled organisms
questions.hint: Think about distance and surface area compared with volume.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Diffusion still happens, but on its own it is too slow over long distances.
B: Incorrect — All living cells need oxygen and nutrients. That's why the systems are needed.
C: Correct — A large organism has a small surface area to volume ratio, so it needs systems to exchange and transport substances.
D: Incorrect — Human cells are a similar size. It's the whole organism that is big.

questions.stem: A student says: "The heart is a tissue because it is made of muscle." Why is the student wrong?
options: The heart is an organ system on its own
The heart contains several tissues, such as muscle, nervous and connective tissue, so it is an organ
The heart is made of only one type of cell, so it is a cell
Muscle is an organ, not a tissue
questions.hint: Is muscle the only thing in the heart?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The heart is one organ. With the blood vessels it forms the circulatory system.
B: Correct — An organ is made of different tissues working together. Muscle is just one of the heart's tissues.
C: Incorrect — The heart is made of many cells of several types.
D: Incorrect — Muscle tissue is a tissue: a group of similar cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about levels of organisation is correct?
options: Plants have no tissues or organs, only cells
One organ can contain several tissues, and one tissue can be found in several organs
Each tissue is found in only one organ
An organ system always contains only one organ
questions.hint: Check each statement against the order: cell, tissue, organ, organ system.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Plants have tissues (e.g. xylem) and organs (e.g. leaves, roots, stems).
B: Correct — e.g. muscle tissue is in the stomach, the heart and the intestine walls, and each of those organs has several tissues.
C: Incorrect — Many tissues, such as muscle and epithelial tissue, are found in several organs.
D: Incorrect — An organ system is a group of organs working together.

questions.stem: Which enzyme breaks down starch into sugars?
options: Protease
Amylase
Lipase
Bile
questions.hint: Its name comes from "amylum", the Latin for starch.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Proteases break down proteins into amino acids.
B: Correct — Amylase is a carbohydrase: it breaks starch down into sugars.
C: Incorrect — Lipases break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.
D: Incorrect — Bile is not an enzyme. It emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid.

questions.stem: Which reagent is used to test a food for protein?
options: Biuret reagent
Limewater
Iodine solution
Benedict's solution
questions.hint: A positive result turns the solution from blue to purple.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple (lilac) if protein is present.
B: Incorrect — Limewater tests for carbon dioxide, not for food.
C: Incorrect — Iodine tests for starch: it turns from orange-brown to blue-black.
D: Incorrect — Benedict's tests for sugars, such as glucose, when heated.

questions.stem: What is the job of red blood cells?
options: To help the blood clot at a wound
To carry dissolved food and hormones
To carry oxygen around the body
To fight pathogens
questions.hint: They contain haemoglobin, which gives them their colour.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the job of platelets.
B: Incorrect — That is mainly done by the plasma.
C: Correct — Haemoglobin joins with oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the body's tissues.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of white blood cells.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart to the body at high pressure?
options: Vena cava
Vein
Artery
Capillary
questions.hint: "A" for "away".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The vena cava is a large vein bringing blood back to the heart from the body.
B: Incorrect — Veins carry blood back to the heart, at low pressure.
C: Correct — Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular, elastic walls to cope with high pressure.
D: Incorrect — Capillaries are tiny vessels where substances are exchanged with the cells.

questions.stem: What is a malignant tumour?
options: A tumour that always disappears on its own
A tumour that invades nearby tissue and can spread through the blood to form secondary tumours
A tumour that stays in one place, usually inside a membrane
A tumour caused by a bacterial infection
questions.hint: Which kind of tumour is cancer?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Malignant tumours don't go away by themselves and need treatment.
B: Correct — Malignant tumours are cancers. They spread to other parts of the body.
C: Incorrect — That describes a benign tumour.
D: Incorrect — Tumours are caused by changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division, not by bacteria.

questions.stem: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. What does it do?
options: It emulsifies fat into small droplets and neutralises stomach acid
It makes the small intestine more acidic
It digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol
It breaks down protein into amino acids
questions.hint: Bile has two jobs: one about fat, one about acid.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Small droplets give lipase a bigger surface area, and the alkaline conditions help lipase work faster.
B: Incorrect — Bile is alkaline. It neutralises the acid from the stomach.
C: Incorrect — Bile isn't an enzyme. Lipase does this digestion.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of protease enzymes.

questions.stem: Using the lock and key model, why does each enzyme only work on one type of substrate?
options: Only a substrate with the right shape fits into the enzyme's active site
Each enzyme is too small to hold more than one molecule
The substrate changes its shape to fit any enzyme
Enzymes are used up after one reaction
questions.hint: Think about the shape of the enzyme's active site.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Like a key in a lock, the substrate must fit the shape of the active site for the reaction to happen.
B: Incorrect — Size isn't the reason. It's the shape of the active site that matters.
C: Incorrect — In the lock and key model, the substrate must already match the active site's shape.
D: Incorrect — Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up and can be reused.

questions.stem: Why is the human circulatory system called a "double" circulatory system?
options: Blood flows in both directions in each vessel
Every organ has two blood vessels going into it
Blood passes through the heart twice on each full journey around the body
The heart has two chambers
questions.hint: Follow one drop of blood all the way round the body.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blood flows one way only. Valves stop it flowing backwards.
B: Incorrect — The "double" refers to two loops through the heart, not to the vessels.
C: Correct — The right side pumps blood to the lungs, and the left side pumps it to the rest of the body.
D: Incorrect — The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.

questions.stem: Capillaries have walls that are only one cell thick. Why is this useful?
options: It stops blood flowing backwards
It lets red blood cells leave the blood easily
It gives a short distance for substances to diffuse between the blood and the cells
It lets them cope with very high blood pressure
questions.hint: What needs to pass between the blood and the body's cells?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Valves in veins stop backflow, not thin walls.
B: Incorrect — Red blood cells stay inside the capillaries. Substances diffuse through the walls.
C: Correct — Oxygen and glucose diffuse out, and waste like carbon dioxide diffuses in, quickly.
D: Incorrect — Thin walls couldn't cope with high pressure. Arteries have thick walls for that.

questions.stem: In coronary heart disease, what goes wrong?
options: The pacemaker cells stop working
The heart valves leak, so blood flows backwards
The red blood cells stop carrying oxygen
Layers of fatty material build up in the coronary arteries, so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle
questions.hint: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That causes an irregular heartbeat, which is treated with an artificial pacemaker.
B: Incorrect — That is a faulty valve, which is a different heart problem.
C: Incorrect — In coronary heart disease the problem is in the arteries, not the blood cells.
D: Correct — The narrowed arteries reduce blood flow, so the heart muscle gets less oxygen.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a lifestyle risk factor to a disease it is linked with?
options: Obesity: Type 2 diabetes
Alcohol: lung cancer
Smoking: Type 2 diabetes
Lack of exercise: skin cancer
questions.hint: Think about which organ each factor damages most.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Obesity is a major risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.
B: Incorrect — Alcohol mainly damages the liver and the brain. Smoking is the main risk factor for lung cancer.
C: Incorrect — Smoking is mainly linked to lung disease, lung cancer and cardiovascular disease.
D: Incorrect — Skin cancer is mainly linked to ionising radiation (UV light), not exercise.

questions.stem: What controls the natural resting heart rate?
options: A group of cells in the left ventricle
A group of pacemaker cells in the right atrium
The coronary arteries
The valves inside the heart
questions.hint: It is a small group of cells in one of the top chambers of the heart.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The natural pacemaker is in the right atrium, not the left ventricle.
B: Correct — These cells send out small electrical impulses that make the heart muscle contract. An artificial pacemaker can correct an irregular rhythm.
C: Incorrect — These supply the heart muscle with oxygen. They don't control the rate.
D: Incorrect — Valves stop blood flowing backwards. They don't set the heart rate.

questions.stem: Which example shows two types of disease interacting?
options: A person who exercises regularly has a lower heart rate
A defect in the immune system makes a person more likely to catch infectious diseases
A person catches a cold and then gets better a week later
A person breaks their leg playing football
questions.hint: Look for one illness making another one more likely.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is an effect of fitness, not a disease interaction.
B: Correct — A weak immune system can't fight pathogens well, so infections become more likely.
C: Incorrect — This is just one disease, with no second disease involved.
D: Incorrect — This is an injury, not two diseases interacting.

questions.stem: In an experiment on the effect of pH on amylase, starch was fully broken down after 120 seconds at pH 6. What is the rate of reaction?
questions.hint: Rate = 1000 ÷ time.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is the time, not the rate. Use rate = 1000 ÷ time.
B: Correct — 1000 ÷ 120 = 8.33, so 8.3 s⁻¹ (to 2 significant figures).
C: Incorrect — This is 120 ÷ 1000, which is the wrong way round.
D: Incorrect — This is 120 × 6. The pH value isn't used in the rate calculation.

questions.stem: Why does amylase stop working when it is heated to a high temperature?
options: The enzyme is killed because it is alive
The starch molecules move too slowly to reach the enzyme
The enzyme gets used up faster at high temperatures
The active site changes shape (the enzyme is denatured), so starch no longer fits
questions.hint: What happens to the shape of the active site?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they can't be killed. They are denatured.
B: Incorrect — Heating makes molecules move faster, not slower.
C: Incorrect — Enzymes aren't used up. It stops working because its shape changes.
D: Correct — High temperatures break the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the substrate can't fit the active site.

questions.stem: Which feature of the alveoli does NOT help gas exchange in the lungs?
options: They have a rich supply of blood capillaries
They give a very large surface area
They are surrounded by thick, muscular walls
Their walls are very thin
questions.hint: Three of these make diffusion faster. One has nothing to do with it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blood flow keeps a steep concentration gradient, so diffusion stays fast.
B: Incorrect — A large surface area lets more oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse at once.
C: Correct — Alveoli have very thin walls (one cell thick). Thick walls would slow diffusion down.
D: Incorrect — Thin walls mean a short diffusion distance.

questions.stem: A doctor offers a patient with coronary heart disease either a stent or statins. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: A stent holds the artery open straight away; statins lower blood cholesterol and slow down further fatty build-up
Statins hold the artery open; a stent lowers blood cholesterol
Both treatments remove all fatty material from every artery
A stent has no risks because it doesn't involve any surgery
questions.hint: One is a device put in an artery; the other is a drug taken for life.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Stents need surgery but work quickly. Statins avoid surgery but must be taken long term and can have side effects.
B: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
C: Incorrect — Neither removes all fat. A stent opens one narrowed section; statins slow further build-up.
D: Incorrect — Fitting a stent involves a procedure with some risks, such as infection or blood clots.

questions.stem: What does xylem tissue transport?
options: Oxygen from the leaves to the roots
Starch from the roots to the leaves
Dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant
Water and mineral ions from the roots to the stem and leaves
questions.hint: It carries things up from the roots.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxygen moves into plant cells by diffusion, not through xylem.
B: Incorrect — Starch is insoluble and is stored, not transported in xylem.
C: Incorrect — That is the job of phloem (translocation).
D: Correct — Xylem carries the transpiration stream upwards from the roots.

questions.stem: What is translocation?
options: The movement of water from the roots to the leaves
The uptake of mineral ions by root hair cells
The movement of dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant
The loss of water vapour from the leaves
questions.hint: It happens in the phloem.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the transpiration stream, in the xylem.
B: Incorrect — Root hair cells take in mineral ions by active transport. That isn't translocation.
C: Correct — Phloem carries sugars made in photosynthesis to where they are used or stored.
D: Incorrect — That is transpiration.

questions.stem: What do guard cells control?
options: The growth of new roots
The opening and closing of the stomata
The movement of sugars in the phloem
The uptake of water by the roots
questions.hint: They sit in pairs around small holes in the leaf.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — New cells are made in meristem tissue at the root and shoot tips.
B: Correct — Guard cells change shape to open and close the stomata, controlling gas exchange and water loss.
C: Incorrect — Guard cells are in the leaf surface and have nothing to do with phloem transport.
D: Incorrect — Root hair cells take in water by osmosis.

questions.stem: Where in a leaf does most photosynthesis happen?
options: Palisade mesophyll
Phloem
Upper epidermis
Xylem
questions.hint: These cells are packed with chloroplasts near the top of the leaf.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Palisade cells are near the upper surface and have lots of chloroplasts to absorb light.
B: Incorrect — Phloem carries dissolved sugars. It doesn't do most of the photosynthesis.
C: Incorrect — The upper epidermis is thin and see-through, so light passes through it. It has few or no chloroplasts.
D: Incorrect — Xylem carries water and mineral ions. Its cells are dead and have no chloroplasts.

questions.stem: What is meristem tissue?
options: Tissue that can divide to make new cells, which can become any type of plant cell
The waxy layer that covers the leaf
Tissue that carries water up the stem
Tissue that carries sugars down the stem
questions.hint: It's found at the growing tips of roots and shoots.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Meristem cells are like plant stem cells, so the plant can grow at its tips.
B: Incorrect — That is the waxy cuticle, made by the epidermis.
C: Incorrect — That is xylem.
D: Incorrect — That is phloem.

questions.stem: How do root hair cells take in mineral ions from the soil?
options: By diffusion down a concentration gradient
By active transport, using energy from respiration
By osmosis
Through the stomata
questions.hint: There are usually more mineral ions inside the root cell than in the soil.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The concentration of ions is usually lower in the soil, so diffusion would move them the wrong way.
B: Correct — The ions move against the concentration gradient, so energy from respiration is needed.
C: Incorrect — Osmosis is the movement of water, not mineral ions. Root hair cells take in water by osmosis.
D: Incorrect — Stomata are in the leaves and let gases in and out, not mineral ions.

questions.stem: Which feature of xylem helps it carry water up the plant?
options: Lots of chloroplasts
Living cells with pores in their end walls
Long thin extensions that stick into the soil
Hollow tubes strengthened by lignin
questions.hint: Think about the shape of the cells and what makes them strong.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Xylem doesn't photosynthesise. Its cells are dead.
B: Incorrect — That describes phloem, not xylem.
C: Incorrect — That describes root hair cells.
D: Correct — The cells have no end walls, so water flows freely, and lignin stops the tubes collapsing.

questions.stem: Which change would make a plant transpire faster?
options: A more humid day
Moving the plant into the dark
A colder day
A windier day
questions.hint: Think about what makes washing on a line dry quickly.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — More water vapour in the air makes the gradient shallower, so transpiration slows down.
B: Incorrect — In the dark most stomata close, so transpiration slows down.
C: Incorrect — Lower temperatures slow evaporation and diffusion, so transpiration slows down.
D: Correct — Moving air carries water vapour away from the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so more water evaporates.

questions.stem: How is the spongy mesophyll adapted for its function?
options: It is packed tightly with no gaps, to catch more light
It is covered in a thick waxy layer to stop gases entering
It has air spaces that let gases diffuse in and out of cells easily
It is made of hollow tubes strengthened with lignin
questions.hint: Think about how carbon dioxide gets to the palisade cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That fits the palisade layer better. The spongy layer is full of gaps.
B: Incorrect — A waxy cuticle reduces water loss from the outside of the leaf. The spongy layer needs gases to move.
C: Correct — The air spaces give a large surface area for carbon dioxide and oxygen to diffuse.
D: Incorrect — That describes xylem.

questions.stem: Why do most stomata close at night?
options: There is no light for photosynthesis, so closing them saves water
So that the plant can take in more carbon dioxide
Because the plant stops respiring at night
To speed up transpiration
questions.hint: What can't the plant do in the dark?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The plant doesn't need to take in carbon dioxide in the dark, so it closes stomata to reduce water loss.
B: Incorrect — Closed stomata let less carbon dioxide in, not more.
C: Incorrect — Plants respire all the time, day and night.
D: Incorrect — Closing the stomata slows transpiration down.

questions.stem: Most stomata are on the lower surface of a leaf. Why is this useful?
options: Water can't evaporate from the lower surface at all
The lower surface is cooler and shaded, so less water is lost by evaporation
The lower surface gets more light for photosynthesis
It helps the leaf take in mineral ions from the air
questions.hint: Which surface is hotter and in direct sunlight?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Water does evaporate from the lower surface. It is just slower there.
B: Correct — Having stomata where it is cooler cuts water loss but still allows gas exchange.
C: Incorrect — The upper surface gets more light. That's why palisade cells are near the top.
D: Incorrect — Mineral ions are taken in by the roots, from the soil.

questions.stem: A potometer shows that a plant took up 1.8 cm³ of water in 15 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake?
options: 27 cm³/min
1.2 cm³/min
0.12 cm³/min
8.3 cm³/min
questions.hint: Rate = volume ÷ time.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is 1.8 × 15. You need to divide, not multiply.
B: Incorrect — Check the decimal place: 1.8 ÷ 15 = 0.12.
C: Correct — 1.8 ÷ 15 = 0.12 cm³ per minute.
D: Incorrect — This is 15 ÷ 1.8, which is the wrong way round.

questions.stem: A potometer measures how fast a plant takes up water. Why is this not exactly the same as its rate of transpiration?
options: Some of the water taken up is used by the plant, e.g. in photosynthesis, so not all of it is lost
Plants lose more water than they take up
Transpiration only happens at night
Water only enters through the leaves, not the stem
questions.hint: Does every drop of water that goes in leave through the leaves?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — A potometer measures water uptake. A small amount is used or kept in cells rather than evaporating.
B: Incorrect — Over time a healthy plant takes up slightly more water than it loses, because some is used.
C: Incorrect — Transpiration happens mostly in the day, when stomata are open.
D: Incorrect — In a potometer the water enters through the cut stem.

questions.stem: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of transpiration.
options: Heat speeds up translocation in the phloem, pulling water up
Water molecules gain energy, so they evaporate and diffuse out of the leaf faster
Heat makes the xylem tubes wider
Warmer air holds less water vapour, so stomata close
questions.hint: Think about how fast water molecules move when they are warmer.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Translocation moves sugars in the phloem. It doesn't pull water up the xylem.
B: Correct — Faster-moving molecules evaporate from cell surfaces and diffuse out through the stomata more quickly.
C: Incorrect — Xylem is strengthened by lignin. Its width doesn't change with temperature.
D: Incorrect — Higher temperatures don't make stomata close for this reason, and closing would slow transpiration.

questions.stem: How do guard cells open a stoma?
options: Muscles in the leaf pull the guard cells apart
The guard cells lose water and shrink, opening the gap between them
Sugars from the phloem push the guard cells apart
Water moves into the guard cells, they swell and become turgid, and they bend apart to open the gap
questions.hint: Think about what happens when water moves into a cell by osmosis.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Plants have no muscles. The change is caused by water moving in or out.
B: Incorrect — When guard cells lose water they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
C: Incorrect — Guard cells open because they take in water by osmosis, not because sugars push them.
D: Correct — When the guard cells are full of water they curve outwards, opening the stoma. When they lose water they become flaccid and close it.

questions.stem: What is a pathogen?
options: Any living thing that lives inside the body
A microorganism that causes an infectious disease
A medicine that kills bacteria
A protein made by white blood cells to fight infection
questions.hint: Think about what causes an infectious disease.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Many microorganisms live in us without causing harm, so they are not pathogens.
B: Correct — Pathogens can be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi.
C: Incorrect — That describes an antibiotic.
D: Incorrect — That describes an antibody, not a pathogen.

questions.stem: Someone has flu, which is caused by a virus. They take painkillers. What will the painkillers do?
options: Kill any bacteria in the body
Kill the flu virus
Make antibodies against the flu virus
Ease symptoms such as aches, but not kill the virus
questions.hint: Think about the difference between treating the symptoms and treating the cause.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Killing bacteria is what antibiotics do, not painkillers.
B: Incorrect — Painkillers do not kill pathogens of any kind.
C: Incorrect — Antibodies are made by white blood cells, not by painkillers.
D: Correct — Painkillers treat the symptoms of a disease. They do not kill pathogens.

questions.stem: How is the measles virus spread from person to person?
options: By breathing in droplets from sneezes and coughs
By a bite from an infected mosquito
By eating undercooked chicken
Only by sexual contact
questions.hint: Measles is caught in a similar way to a cold.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The measles virus is carried in tiny droplets that other people inhale.
B: Incorrect — That is how malaria is spread.
C: Incorrect — That is a common way to catch Salmonella food poisoning.
D: Incorrect — That is how gonorrhoea and HIV are spread, not measles.

questions.stem: Why will a doctor not give antibiotics for a cold caused by a virus?
options: Antibiotics would make the virus reproduce faster
Antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses
Antibiotics only work on diseases in plants
Colds are caused by bacteria that are too strong for antibiotics
questions.hint: Antibiotics only work on one type of pathogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibiotics simply have no effect on viruses. They don't speed them up.
B: Correct — Antibiotics such as penicillin kill bacteria. They have no effect on viral pathogens.
C: Incorrect — Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial diseases in humans and animals.
D: Incorrect — Colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria.

questions.stem: How does the stomach help defend the body against pathogens?
options: It makes antibodies that stick to pathogens
It forms a waterproof barrier over the body
It makes acid that kills most pathogens we swallow
It makes sticky mucus with cilia that sweep pathogens away
questions.hint: Think about what the stomach makes that would harm most microorganisms.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibodies are made by white blood cells.
B: Incorrect — That describes the skin.
C: Correct — Stomach acid kills most of the pathogens that get in with food and drink.
D: Incorrect — That describes the trachea and bronchi, not the stomach.

questions.stem: Malaria is caused by a protist carried by mosquitoes. Which of these helps stop malaria spreading?
options: Covering your mouth when you cough
Washing your hands before cooking food
Using a condom
Sleeping under a mosquito net
questions.hint: Think about how the pathogen gets into a person.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That helps stop diseases spread in droplets, like measles, but malaria is spread by mosquito bites.
B: Incorrect — That helps stop food poisoning such as Salmonella.
C: Incorrect — That helps stop sexually transmitted diseases, not malaria.
D: Correct — Nets stop people being bitten. Stopping mosquitoes breeding also helps.

questions.stem: Which drug was first found in foxglove plants?
options: Penicillin
Digitalis
Aspirin
Morphine
questions.hint: It is a heart drug.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
B: Correct — The heart drug digitalis comes from foxgloves.
C: Incorrect — The painkiller aspirin comes from willow.
D: Incorrect — Morphine comes from the opium poppy, not foxgloves.

questions.stem: What happens if HIV is not controlled with antiretroviral drugs?
options: The virus attacks the immune cells, so in time the body can't fight off other infections or cancers
The person gets a fever and a red skin rash
The body makes far too many white blood cells
The virus is killed by the body's stomach acid
questions.hint: Think about which cells the virus attacks.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This late stage of HIV infection is called AIDS.
B: Incorrect — Those are the symptoms of measles.
C: Incorrect — HIV destroys immune cells. It doesn't make extra ones.
D: Incorrect — HIV is spread by sexual contact and body fluids such as blood, so stomach acid doesn't stop it.

questions.stem: Why does a tomato plant infected with tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) grow less well?
options: Discoloured patches on the leaves mean less photosynthesis
The virus eats the roots
Purple and black spots make the leaves drop off
The virus blocks the xylem so no water reaches the leaves
questions.hint: Look at what the virus does to the colour of the leaves.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — TMV causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration, so the plant makes less food for growth.
B: Incorrect — Viruses don't eat anything. They reproduce inside cells.
C: Incorrect — That describes rose black spot, a fungal disease.
D: Incorrect — TMV affects the leaves' colour. It doesn't block the xylem.

questions.stem: Which of these is done in the UK to control the spread of Salmonella?
options: Vaccinating poultry such as chickens
Giving all children antibiotics before meals
Spraying fungicide on crops
Giving everyone mosquito nets
questions.hint: Think about where Salmonella food poisoning often comes from.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Chickens are vaccinated so they are less likely to carry Salmonella into our food.
B: Incorrect — This is not done. Overusing antibiotics would help resistant bacteria spread.
C: Incorrect — Salmonella is a bacterium, not a fungus.
D: Incorrect — Mosquito nets help stop malaria, which is spread by mosquitoes.

questions.stem: Gonorrhoea used to be easy to treat with penicillin. Why is it harder to treat now?
options: Gonorrhoea is now spread through the air
Penicillin is no longer made
Many strains of the bacterium have become resistant to penicillin
Gonorrhoea is now caused by a virus
questions.hint: Think about how bacteria can change over time.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gonorrhoea is spread by sexual contact.
B: Incorrect — Penicillin is still made. The problem is resistance.
C: Correct — Resistant strains are not killed by penicillin, so other antibiotics are needed.
D: Incorrect — Gonorrhoea is still caused by a bacterium.

questions.stem: A gardener finds black spots on the leaves of a rose bush. How should they treat it?
options: Spray it with fungicide and remove and destroy the affected leaves
Spray it with antibiotics
Give it more water
Vaccinate the rose bush
questions.hint: Think about what type of pathogen causes this disease.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Rose black spot is caused by a fungus, so fungicides work. Removing the leaves stops spores spreading.
B: Incorrect — Antibiotics kill bacteria, not fungi.
C: Incorrect — The spores are spread by water and wind, so more water won't cure it.
D: Incorrect — Plants are not vaccinated against black spot.

questions.stem: How do the trachea and bronchi help stop pathogens reaching the lungs?
options: They close up whenever a pathogen enters
They make acid that kills the pathogens
They make sticky mucus that traps pathogens, and cilia move it up to the throat
They make antitoxins
questions.hint: Think about what lines the airways.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The airways stay open. Mucus and cilia do the work.
B: Incorrect — That is how the stomach defends the body.
C: Correct — The trapped pathogens are then swallowed or coughed out.
D: Incorrect — Antitoxins are made by white blood cells.

questions.stem: What does a vaccine contain?
options: Small amounts of a dead or inactive form of the pathogen
Large amounts of the live, active pathogen
Antibiotics
Painkillers
questions.hint: It has to make white blood cells respond without making you ill.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This makes white blood cells produce antibodies without causing the disease.
B: Incorrect — That would be likely to cause the disease.
C: Incorrect — Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria. They are not vaccines.
D: Incorrect — Painkillers treat symptoms. They don't train the immune system.

questions.stem: Which list shows the correct order for testing a new drug?
options: Tested on cells, tissues and animals → low doses given to healthy volunteers → trials on patients to find the best dose
Low doses given to healthy volunteers → tested on cells, tissues and animals → trials on patients
Tested on cells, tissues and animals → trials on patients → low doses given to healthy volunteers
Trials on patients → tested on cells, tissues and animals → low doses given to healthy volunteers
questions.hint: The drug must be shown to be safe before it is given to anyone who is ill.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Preclinical testing comes first, then clinical trials starting with very low doses.
B: Incorrect — Preclinical testing in the lab must come before any people take the drug.
C: Incorrect — Healthy volunteers are tested with low doses before patients, to check safety.
D: Incorrect — Patients are only given the drug once it has been shown to be safe.

questions.stem: Some bacteria release toxins. How do white blood cells deal with the toxins?
options: They make mucus to trap the toxins
They make antibiotics
They make stomach acid
They make antitoxins that cancel out the toxins
questions.hint: Look for a word that sounds like the opposite of a toxin.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Mucus is made in the airways, not by white blood cells.
B: Incorrect — Antibiotics are medicines. The body doesn't make them.
C: Incorrect — Stomach acid is made by the stomach, not white blood cells.
D: Correct — Antitoxin production is one of the three ways white blood cells defend the body.

questions.stem: A vaccinated person later meets the real pathogen. Why are they unlikely to become ill?
options: Antibodies from the vaccine stay in the blood forever
Their white blood cells respond quickly and make the correct antibodies
The vaccine has made the pathogen resistant
The vaccine stops the pathogen getting through the skin
questions.hint: Think about how fast the body can react the second time.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A vaccine contains a dead or inactive pathogen, not antibodies.
B: Correct — The pathogen is destroyed before it can make the person ill.
C: Incorrect — Resistance helps pathogens, not people. It has nothing to do with vaccines working.
D: Incorrect — A vaccine works through the immune system, not the skin.

questions.stem: Some people can't be vaccinated. Why does vaccinating most of the population still help protect them?
options: The pathogen becomes weaker each time it meets a vaccinated person
Fewer people can catch and pass on the pathogen, so it spreads less
Unvaccinated people breathe in antibodies from vaccinated people
The vaccine spreads from vaccinated people to others
questions.hint: Think about how a pathogen gets from one person to another.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Vaccination doesn't weaken the pathogen. It stops it spreading.
B: Correct — If most people are immune, the pathogen is less likely to reach the unvaccinated.
C: Incorrect — Antibodies are not passed on in the air.
D: Incorrect — The vaccine stays in the person who was given it.

questions.stem: In a double-blind drug trial, some patients are given a placebo. Who knows which patients got the placebo?
options: The doctors know, but the patients don't
Everyone in the trial knows
The patients know, but the doctors don't
Neither the doctors nor the patients, until the trial is over
questions.hint: "Double" means two groups of people are kept in the dark.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Then only the patients are "blind", so it isn't double-blind.
B: Incorrect — Then the trial isn't blind at all.
C: Incorrect — In a double-blind trial the patients don't know either.
D: Correct — This stops anyone's expectations affecting the results.

questions.stem: Why is it hard to develop drugs that kill viruses?
options: Viruses don't cause any damage, so there is no need
Viruses have tough cellulose cell walls
Viruses live inside the body's cells, so a drug that kills them may also damage the body's tissues
Viruses are too large for drugs to get into
questions.hint: Think about where viruses live and reproduce.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Viruses do cause damage: they reproduce inside cells and damage them.
B: Incorrect — Viruses don't have cell walls at all. Cellulose cell walls are found in plants.
C: Correct — Viruses reproduce inside our cells, which makes them hard to reach safely.
D: Incorrect — Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how bacteria and viruses make us ill?
options: Both only make us ill by using up our food
Bacteria and viruses cannot reproduce inside the body
Viruses release toxins; bacteria reproduce inside our cells
Bacteria may release toxins that damage tissues; viruses reproduce inside cells and damage them
questions.hint: One of them may release poisons. The other has to get inside our cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Neither works mainly this way. Toxins and cell damage make us ill.
B: Incorrect — Both can reproduce rapidly inside the body.
C: Incorrect — This swaps the two round.
D: Correct — Both can reproduce quickly in the body, but they cause damage in different ways.

questions.stem: Monoclonal antibodies are made from...
options: Bacteria
Plant cells
A single clone of identical cells
Many different types of white blood cell
questions.hint: "Mono" means one.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Monoclonal antibodies are made by hybridoma cells, not bacteria.
B: Incorrect — They are made using mouse lymphocytes and tumour cells.
C: Correct — All the cells are copies of one cell, so they all make the same antibody.
D: Incorrect — Different white blood cells would make many different antibodies.

questions.stem: Which cells are first stimulated to make the antibody when producing monoclonal antibodies?
options: Human skin cells
Mouse red blood cells
Tumour cells
Mouse lymphocytes
questions.hint: These are white blood cells taken from an animal.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Skin cells don't make antibodies.
B: Incorrect — Red blood cells carry oxygen. They don't make antibodies.
C: Incorrect — Tumour cells are added later because they divide a lot, but they don't make the antibody.
D: Correct — Lymphocytes are white blood cells that make antibodies.

questions.stem: Which of these is a use of monoclonal antibodies?
options: Killing the virus that causes a cold
Making plants grow faster
Replacing antibiotics for all bacterial infections
Pregnancy tests
questions.hint: Think about tests that look for one particular chemical.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Monoclonal antibodies are not used as cold cures.
B: Incorrect — Monoclonal antibodies are not used as plant fertilisers.
C: Incorrect — Antibiotics are still used to treat bacterial infections.
D: Correct — The antibodies stick to a hormone found only in the urine of pregnant women.

questions.stem: What is a hybridoma cell?
options: A tumour cell that has been killed
A virus living inside a lymphocyte
A lymphocyte combined with a tumour cell
A lymphocyte combined with a red blood cell
questions.hint: "Hybrid" means a mix of two things.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The tumour cell is combined with a lymphocyte, not killed.
B: Incorrect — No virus is involved.
C: Correct — The hybridoma cell can both make the antibody and divide again and again.
D: Incorrect — A red blood cell is not used. It is a tumour cell.

questions.stem: Why is a lymphocyte combined with a tumour cell to make monoclonal antibodies?
options: Tumour cells make the antibody radioactive
Tumour cells kill the pathogen
Tumour cells make the antibody
Tumour cells divide again and again, so the hybridoma can divide as well as make the antibody
questions.hint: Think about what tumour cells are good at.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibodies can be attached to radioactive substances later, but that isn't why tumour cells are used.
B: Incorrect — The tumour cell is only there to help the cells divide.
C: Incorrect — The lymphocyte makes the antibody. The tumour cell lets it divide.
D: Correct — On their own, lymphocytes that make antibodies don't divide well.

questions.stem: Why does a monoclonal antibody target only one type of cell or chemical?
options: It is made by many different cells
It is specific to one binding site on one protein antigen
It is too large to fit onto other cells
It kills every other cell it meets
questions.hint: Think about how antibodies fit onto antigens.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — It is made by a single clone of cells, which is why every antibody is the same.
B: Correct — Its shape only fits that one antigen, so it only sticks to that target.
C: Incorrect — Size isn't the reason. Its shape matches one antigen.
D: Incorrect — It doesn't attack other cells. It just doesn't bind to them.

questions.stem: How can monoclonal antibodies help scientists find where a particular molecule is in a tissue?
options: A fluorescent dye is attached to the antibodies, which bind to the molecule and make it glow
The antibodies digest the molecule so it disappears
The antibodies make the molecule divide
The antibodies change colour when the tissue is heated
questions.hint: They need a way to make the antibody visible.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The glow shows exactly where the molecule is.
B: Incorrect — Antibodies bind to molecules. They don't digest them.
C: Incorrect — Molecules don't divide. The antibody just binds to it.
D: Incorrect — The colour comes from the attached dye, not from heating.

questions.stem: How can monoclonal antibodies be used to treat cancer?
options: A drug or radioactive substance is attached, and the antibody carries it to the cancer cells only
They kill every fast-dividing cell in the body
They bind to all cells, healthy and cancerous
They act like antibiotics and kill cancer bacteria
questions.hint: Think about how the antibody finds its target.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This damages the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.
B: Incorrect — They bind only to cells with the matching antigen.
C: Incorrect — They are specific, so they only bind to their target.
D: Incorrect — Cancer is not caused by bacteria, and these are not antibiotics.
