questions.stem: Which of these is a way monoclonal antibodies are used in hospital laboratories?
options: Growing cultures of bacteria faster
Measuring a patient's blood pressure
Killing bacteria on lab equipment
Measuring the levels of hormones in blood, or detecting pathogens
questions.hint: They can stick to one particular chemical in a blood sample.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Monoclonal antibodies are not used to help bacteria grow.
B: Incorrect — Blood pressure is measured with a cuff, not antibodies.
C: Incorrect — Equipment is sterilised with heat or disinfectant, not antibodies.
D: Correct — Because the antibody binds to one target, it can show whether that target is there.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order for making monoclonal antibodies?
options: Combine with tumour cells → stimulate mouse lymphocytes → collect the antibody → clone a single hybridoma
Stimulate mouse lymphocytes → collect and purify the antibody → combine with tumour cells → clone a single hybridoma
Stimulate mouse lymphocytes → combine with tumour cells to make hybridomas → clone a single hybridoma → collect and purify the antibody
Clone a single hybridoma → stimulate mouse lymphocytes → combine with tumour cells → collect the antibody
questions.hint: The cells must make the right antibody before they are fused.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The lymphocytes are stimulated before they are fused, and cloning comes before collection.
B: Incorrect — Large amounts of antibody are only made after the hybridoma is cloned.
C: Correct — The lymphocytes are triggered to make the antibody first, then made able to divide.
D: Incorrect — You can't clone a hybridoma before it has been made.

questions.stem: Why are monoclonal antibodies not yet as widely used as people hoped?
options: They bind to every cell in the body
Only tiny amounts can ever be made
Bacteria quickly become resistant to them
They have caused more side effects than expected
questions.hint: Think about what happened when they were used in patients.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — They are specific to one antigen.
B: Incorrect — Cloned hybridoma cells make large amounts, which can be collected and purified.
C: Incorrect — Resistance is a problem with antibiotics, not the reason here.
D: Correct — This has limited their use in treatment.

questions.stem: A pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies with a coloured dye attached. They bind to a hormone called HCG, which is only in the urine of pregnant women. Why does a coloured line appear only if the woman is pregnant?
options: The antibodies make HCG when urine touches them
The antibodies destroy HCG, leaving a coloured mark
The antibodies change colour in any urine
The antibodies are specific to HCG, so they only bind and show colour when HCG is present
questions.hint: Ask yourself what the antibodies can stick to.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibodies don't make hormones. They bind to them.
B: Incorrect — The line appears because the antibodies bind to HCG, not because they destroy it.
C: Incorrect — Then every test would show a line, pregnant or not.
D: Correct — No HCG means nothing for the antibodies to bind to, so no line forms.

questions.stem: Which of these is a physical defence that helps a plant stop microorganisms getting in?
options: Poisons in the leaves
Thorns on the stem
Antibacterial chemicals
A tough, waxy cuticle on the leaves
questions.hint: Physical defences are barriers.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence against herbivores.
B: Incorrect — That is a mechanical defence against animals.
C: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence, not a physical one.
D: Correct — The cuticle is a barrier that microorganisms find hard to get through.

questions.stem: How do thorns help a plant?
options: They store water
They deter animals from eating the plant
They kill bacteria
They absorb extra light for photosynthesis
questions.hint: Think about what would happen to an animal that tried to eat it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Thorns don't store water.
B: Correct — Thorns are a mechanical defence. Hairs do a similar job.
C: Incorrect — Plants use antibacterial chemicals for that.
D: Incorrect — Leaves absorb light. Thorns are for defence.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that a plant may have a disease?
options: Roots growing downwards
Flowers opening in the sunshine
Leaves growing towards the light
Spots on the leaves
questions.hint: Look for something that has gone wrong with the plant.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is normal, healthy growth.
B: Incorrect — This is normal for many flowering plants.
C: Incorrect — This is normal, healthy growth.
D: Correct — Spots, rot, growths, discolouration and stunted growth can all be signs of disease.

questions.stem: Aphids are small animals that feed on plants. What kind of plant problem are they?
options: Insect pests
A fungus
An ion deficiency
A virus
questions.hint: Think about what kind of living thing an aphid is.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Aphids are insects. Seeing pests on a plant is a sign it may be damaged or diseased.
B: Incorrect — Rose black spot is an example of a fungal disease. Aphids are insects.
C: Incorrect — Ion deficiencies are caused by a lack of minerals, not by animals.
D: Incorrect — Viruses are not animals. TMV is an example of a plant virus.

questions.stem: A plant's leaves have turned yellow because it can't make enough chlorophyll. Which ion is most likely to be missing from the soil?
options: Glucose
Nitrate
Magnesium
Oxygen
questions.hint: This yellowing is called chlorosis.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glucose is not an ion, and the plant makes it by photosynthesis.
B: Incorrect — A lack of nitrate causes stunted growth, because nitrate is needed for proteins.
C: Correct — Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, so a lack causes chlorosis.
D: Incorrect — Oxygen is not taken from the soil as an ion.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to find out exactly which pathogen is infecting a crop. Which method could they use?
options: Count the stomata on a leaf
Use a testing kit containing monoclonal antibodies
Water the plant more and see if it recovers
Spray antibiotics and see if the plant recovers
questions.hint: Think about tests that can recognise one particular pathogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stomata numbers don't tell you which pathogen is present.
B: Correct — The antibodies bind only to the matching pathogen, so the kit can identify it.
C: Incorrect — This wouldn't identify the pathogen.
D: Incorrect — This wouldn't identify the pathogen, and antibiotics don't work on viruses or fungi.

questions.stem: Some plants make poisons in their leaves. How does this help the plant?
options: It helps the leaves absorb more light
It attracts insects to pollinate the flowers
It deters herbivores from eating it
It stops water being lost from the leaves
questions.hint: Think about which animals eat leaves.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Poisons don't affect how much light is absorbed.
B: Incorrect — Poisons put animals off. They don't attract them.
C: Correct — Poisons are a chemical defence against animals that eat plants.
D: Incorrect — That is the job of the waxy cuticle and the stomata.

questions.stem: Some plants have leaves that droop or curl when they are touched. How might this help the plant?
options: It makes the leaves photosynthesise faster
It kills bacteria on the leaf
It helps the plant take in more carbon dioxide
It can knock off insects or scare away animals that might eat it
questions.hint: Think about an insect or animal landing on the leaf.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Drooping leaves would get less light, not more.
B: Incorrect — Plants use antibacterial chemicals to kill bacteria.
C: Incorrect — Curling leaves doesn't help take in carbon dioxide.
D: Correct — This is a mechanical defence.

questions.stem: How does a cellulose cell wall help a plant resist disease?
options: It makes poisons to deter herbivores
It makes antibodies
It is a tough barrier that makes it harder for microorganisms to get into the cell
It releases chemicals that kill bacteria
questions.hint: Is this a physical, chemical or mechanical defence?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence.
B: Incorrect — Plants don't make antibodies.
C: Correct — Cellulose cell walls are a physical defence.
D: Incorrect — That is a chemical defence. Cellulose works as a barrier.

questions.stem: Why does a plant that is short of nitrate ions show stunted growth?
options: Nitrate is needed to open the stomata
Nitrate is needed to make chlorophyll
Nitrate is needed to make proteins, which are needed for growth
Nitrate is needed to make glucose
questions.hint: Think about which large molecules contain nitrogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Stomata open when guard cells take in water.
B: Incorrect — That is magnesium. A lack of magnesium causes yellow leaves.
C: Correct — Without enough nitrate the plant can't make enough protein, so it stays small.
D: Incorrect — Glucose is made by photosynthesis from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.stem: The bark on a tree is made of layers of dead cells that fall off. How does this help defend the tree?
options: It is a barrier, and any microorganisms on it fall away with the dead cells
The dead cells release poisons to deter herbivores
The dead cells make antibodies
The dead cells photosynthesise to make extra food
questions.hint: Think about what happens to anything sitting on the outside.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This is a physical defence that resists invasion by microorganisms.
B: Incorrect — Poisons are a chemical defence. Bark works as a barrier.
C: Incorrect — Plants don't make antibodies.
D: Incorrect — Dead cells can't photosynthesise.

questions.stem: A tomato plant is growing slowly and its leaves have a patchy pattern of light and dark green. A soil test shows normal nitrate and magnesium levels. What is the most likely cause?
options: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)
Rose black spot
Magnesium deficiency
Nitrate deficiency
questions.hint: The soil test rules out two of the options.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — TMV gives a mosaic pattern on the leaves, which reduces photosynthesis and growth.
B: Incorrect — Black spot causes purple or black spots on leaves, not a light and dark green mosaic.
C: Incorrect — The soil test shows magnesium is normal.
D: Incorrect — The soil test shows nitrate is normal.

questions.stem: Which word equation shows photosynthesis?
options: carbon dioxide + oxygen → glucose + water
glucose + water → carbon dioxide + oxygen
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
questions.hint: Think about what a plant takes in from the air and the soil, and what it gives out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, not something the plant uses up to make glucose.
B: Incorrect — Glucose is made in photosynthesis, not used up.
C: Correct — Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and use light energy to make glucose, giving off oxygen.
D: Incorrect — This is aerobic respiration, the reverse of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction. What does this mean?
options: Energy is taken in from the surroundings, as light, by the chloroplasts
Energy is given out to the surroundings as heat
No energy is transferred at all
It can only happen when the plant is warm
questions.hint: "Endo" means "in".
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Endothermic reactions take in energy. In photosynthesis light energy is transferred to the chloroplasts.
B: Incorrect — That describes an exothermic reaction, such as respiration.
C: Incorrect — Photosynthesis needs a supply of light energy to happen.
D: Incorrect — Endothermic is about energy being taken in, not about the temperature it needs.

questions.stem: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis happen?
options: Nucleus
Cell wall
Mitochondria
Chloroplasts
questions.hint: This part is green.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The nucleus holds the genetic material that controls the cell.
B: Incorrect — The cell wall is made of cellulose and strengthens the cell.
C: Incorrect — Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens.
D: Correct — Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the light needed for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which substance in leaves absorbs light for photosynthesis?
options: Chlorophyll
Starch
Cellulose
Glucose
questions.hint: It is what makes leaves green.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy.
B: Incorrect — Starch is how plants store glucose. It doesn't absorb light for photosynthesis.
C: Incorrect — Cellulose makes up the cell wall.
D: Incorrect — Glucose is a product of photosynthesis, not what absorbs light.

questions.stem: A plant is moved from a dim corner to a bright windowsill. Nothing else changes. What will most likely happen to its rate of photosynthesis?
options: It will decrease, because bright light stops photosynthesis
It will increase, because more light energy is available
It will stop, because the plant will run out of water straight away
It will stay the same, because light does not affect photosynthesis
questions.hint: Think about what supplies the energy for photosynthesis.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Brighter light speeds photosynthesis up, until another factor stops it rising further.
B: Correct — When light is low, more light means faster photosynthesis.
C: Incorrect — Moving into brighter light doesn't make the plant run out of water straight away.
D: Incorrect — Light intensity is one of the main factors that affect the rate.

questions.stem: How do plants store glucose that they don't need straight away?
options: As glycogen
As cellulose
As starch
As oxygen
questions.hint: Potatoes are full of this store.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glycogen is how animals, not plants, store glucose.
B: Incorrect — Cellulose is used to build cell walls, not as a store.
C: Correct — Glucose is turned into starch for storage. Plants can also store it as fats or oils.
D: Incorrect — Oxygen is a waste product of photosynthesis. It is not a store of glucose.

questions.stem: Which balanced symbol equation shows photosynthesis?
options: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
6CO₂ + 6O₂ → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂
questions.hint: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. Check which side it is on and that the atoms balance.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is aerobic respiration, the reverse of photosynthesis.
B: Incorrect — Oxygen is made in photosynthesis. Water, not oxygen, is a reactant.
C: Correct — Six carbon dioxide and six water make one glucose and six oxygen. The atoms balance on both sides.
D: Incorrect — These are the right substances, but the equation is not balanced.

questions.stem: The rate of photosynthesis rises as temperature rises, but drops sharply above about 40 °C. Why does it drop?
options: The chlorophyll melts
There is too much light for the plant to use
The carbon dioxide in the air is used up
The enzymes that control photosynthesis are denatured
questions.hint: Photosynthesis is controlled by proteins that change shape when too hot.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorophyll doesn't melt. The drop is caused by enzymes being denatured.
B: Incorrect — Temperature, not light, is what changed here.
C: Incorrect — Warming doesn't use up the carbon dioxide in the air.
D: Correct — High temperatures change the shape of the enzymes' active sites, so they stop working.

questions.stem: A graph shows that the rate of photosynthesis rises as light intensity increases, then levels off. Why does it level off?
options: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide or temperature, is now limiting the rate
Bright light has denatured the enzymes
The plant has started respiring instead of photosynthesising
The plant has run out of chlorophyll
questions.hint: If more light no longer helps, something else must be holding the rate back.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Once light is no longer the limiting factor, the rate is held back by something else that is in short supply.
B: Incorrect — High temperature denatures enzymes, not bright light.
C: Incorrect — Plants respire all the time. Respiration doesn't make photosynthesis level off.
D: Incorrect — The amount of chlorophyll doesn't suddenly run out as light increases.

questions.stem: Some leaves have white patches. Why do the white parts of the leaf not photosynthesise?
options: They are too cold
They get no carbon dioxide
They have no water
They have no chlorophyll to absorb light
questions.hint: Think about what gives a leaf its green colour.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The white parts are the same temperature as the green parts.
B: Incorrect — Carbon dioxide reaches all parts of the leaf by diffusion.
C: Incorrect — Water reaches the whole leaf through the xylem.
D: Correct — Without chlorophyll the cells can't absorb light energy, so the amount of chlorophyll affects the rate.

questions.stem: In the pondweed practical, a lamp is placed at different distances from the pondweed. What is a good way to measure the rate of photosynthesis?
options: Measure the temperature of the water every minute
Count the number of leaves on the pondweed
Measure how much the pondweed grows in length per minute
Count the oxygen bubbles given off per minute, or collect the gas and measure its volume
questions.hint: Pondweed gives off a gas you can see in water.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Temperature is a control variable here. It doesn't measure the rate.
B: Incorrect — The number of leaves doesn't change during the experiment.
C: Incorrect — Pondweed grows far too slowly to measure like this in a lesson.
D: Correct — The faster the pondweed photosynthesises, the more oxygen it gives off each minute.

questions.stem: In the pondweed practical, why might a clear tank of water be put between the lamp and the pondweed?
options: To give the pondweed extra carbon dioxide
To stop heat from the lamp changing the temperature, so only light intensity changes
To make the light brighter
To give the pondweed water for photosynthesis
questions.hint: Lamps don't only give out light.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Plain water doesn't add carbon dioxide. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is used for that.
B: Correct — Temperature also affects the rate, so it must be kept the same to make it a fair test.
C: Incorrect — The water doesn't make the light brighter.
D: Incorrect — The pondweed is already in water.

questions.stem: Plants use glucose and one other substance absorbed from the soil to make amino acids. What is the other substance?
options: Chlorophyll
Nitrate ions
Starch
Oxygen
questions.hint: Farmers add it to fields in fertiliser.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Chlorophyll is made in the plant. It isn't absorbed from the soil.
B: Correct — Nitrate ions supply the nitrogen needed to turn glucose into amino acids, which are built into proteins.
C: Incorrect — Starch is made from glucose. It doesn't come from the soil.
D: Incorrect — Plants make oxygen in photosynthesis. It doesn't provide the nitrogen in amino acids.

questions.stem: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away from a plant. Using the inverse square law, what happens to the light intensity reaching the plant?
options: It falls to a half
It falls to a quarter
It doubles
It stays the same
questions.hint: Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance². The distance has doubled.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would be true if intensity fell in step with distance, but it falls with distance squared.
B: Correct — Doubling the distance gives 1 ÷ 2² = 1/4 of the light intensity.
C: Incorrect — Moving the lamp further away lowers the light intensity.
D: Incorrect — Light spreads out as it travels, so less reaches the plant from further away.

questions.stem: Two plants are kept at the same temperature: one in 0.04% carbon dioxide, one in 0.1% carbon dioxide. In dim light they photosynthesise at exactly the same rate. What is limiting the rate in dim light?
options: Light intensity
Carbon dioxide concentration
The amount of oxygen
The amount of glucose
questions.hint: If extra carbon dioxide made no difference, carbon dioxide can't be what is holding the rate back.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Extra carbon dioxide doesn't help, so light is the factor in short supply. Brighter light would speed both plants up.
B: Incorrect — If carbon dioxide were limiting, the plant with more of it would photosynthesise faster.
C: Incorrect — Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, not a limiting factor.
D: Incorrect — Glucose is a product of photosynthesis, not a limiting factor.

questions.stem: A grower pays to add carbon dioxide to a greenhouse. The rate of photosynthesis rises at first, then stops rising even though more carbon dioxide is added. What is the best decision?
options: Turn off the lights to save money, because light is not needed
Add even more carbon dioxide, because the rate will rise again
Stop adding more carbon dioxide, because another factor is now limiting and the extra only adds cost
Remove all the carbon dioxide, because it is now harmful
questions.hint: Ask what the extra carbon dioxide is buying once the rate stops rising.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Light is needed for photosynthesis, and it may be the factor now limiting the rate.
B: Incorrect — The rate has levelled off because something else is limiting, so more carbon dioxide won't help.
C: Correct — Past this point the extra carbon dioxide costs money without making the crop grow faster. Light or temperature is now limiting.
D: Incorrect — Plants need carbon dioxide to photosynthesise at all.

questions.stem: Why do plants store glucose as starch rather than keeping it as glucose?
options: Starch is insoluble, so it doesn't draw water into cells by osmosis
Starch releases more energy than glucose in respiration
Starch can be used to make chlorophyll
Glucose is poisonous to plant cells
questions.hint: Think about which one dissolves in water, and what that does to water moving in and out of cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Lots of dissolved glucose would make cells take in water by osmosis. Insoluble starch avoids this.
B: Incorrect — Starch has to be broken back down to glucose before it can be used in respiration.
C: Incorrect — Starch is a store of glucose, not used to make chlorophyll.
D: Incorrect — Glucose isn't poisonous. It is used in respiration all the time.

questions.stem: Which word equation shows aerobic respiration?
options: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
glucose → lactic acid
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
questions.hint: "Aerobic" means "with oxygen".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is photosynthesis.
B: Incorrect — This is anaerobic respiration in muscles.
C: Correct — Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, making carbon dioxide and water.
D: Incorrect — This is anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells.

questions.stem: Why is respiration described as an exothermic reaction?
options: It only happens outside cells
It needs oxygen
It takes in light energy
It transfers energy to the surroundings
questions.hint: "Exo" means "out".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Respiration happens inside living cells, all the time.
B: Incorrect — Anaerobic respiration doesn't need oxygen, but it is still exothermic.
C: Incorrect — Taking in light energy describes photosynthesis, which is endothermic.
D: Correct — Respiration releases energy, which cells use for living processes. Some is lost as heat.

questions.stem: What is made when human muscle cells respire anaerobically?
options: Lactic acid
Lactic acid and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide and water
Ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.hint: It is a single product, and it makes muscles ache.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — In muscles, anaerobic respiration is glucose → lactic acid.
B: Incorrect — Anaerobic respiration in muscles makes lactic acid only, no carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — These are made by aerobic respiration.
D: Incorrect — These are made by anaerobic respiration in yeast and plant cells, not muscles.

questions.stem: What is anaerobic respiration in yeast called?
options: Photosynthesis
Digestion
Diffusion
Fermentation
questions.hint: Brewers and bakers rely on it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Yeast is a fungus and can't photosynthesise.
B: Incorrect — Digestion is breaking down large food molecules into small ones.
C: Incorrect — Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from high to low concentration.
D: Correct — Fermentation in yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide. It is used to make bread and alcoholic drinks.

questions.stem: What happens to your heart rate and breathing rate during exercise?
options: Both increase
Both decrease
Heart rate increases but breathing rate decreases
Breathing rate increases but heart rate stays the same
questions.hint: Your muscles need more of something carried by the blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — More oxygenated blood reaches the muscles, and more carbon dioxide is removed.
B: Incorrect — Working muscles need more oxygen, not less.
C: Incorrect — Breathing rate also increases, to take in more oxygen.
D: Incorrect — Heart rate also increases, to pump blood to the muscles faster.

questions.stem: What is metabolism?
options: How fast your heart beats
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body
Only respiration
Only the breakdown of food in the stomach
questions.hint: It covers every reaction, not just one.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is heart rate, not metabolism.
B: Correct — Metabolism includes respiration and all the reactions that make and break down molecules.
C: Incorrect — Respiration is one part of metabolism, but there are many other reactions.
D: Incorrect — That is part of digestion. Metabolism is every reaction in a cell or the body.

questions.stem: Why does anaerobic respiration transfer much less energy than aerobic respiration?
options: It makes more carbon dioxide, which wastes energy
It happens in the chloroplasts instead of the mitochondria
The glucose is only partly broken down (incompletely oxidised)
It doesn't use glucose at all
questions.hint: Think about how much of the glucose is broken down.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Anaerobic respiration in muscles makes no carbon dioxide.
B: Incorrect — Chloroplasts are for photosynthesis, not respiration.
C: Correct — Without oxygen, glucose isn't fully broken down. Lactic acid still holds a lot of energy.
D: Incorrect — Anaerobic respiration does use glucose.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for aerobic respiration but NOT for anaerobic respiration in muscles?
options: It transfers less energy
It uses glucose
It uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water
It makes lactic acid
questions.hint: Compare what each one needs and what each one makes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Aerobic respiration transfers much more energy than anaerobic.
B: Incorrect — Both types of respiration use glucose.
C: Correct — Anaerobic respiration in muscles uses no oxygen and makes only lactic acid.
D: Incorrect — Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration, not aerobic.

questions.stem: Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added?
options: Yeast makes carbon dioxide gas during fermentation, which forms bubbles in the dough
Yeast makes oxygen gas
Yeast makes lactic acid, which makes the dough swell
Water in the dough turns to steam as the yeast grows
questions.hint: Think about the gas made in fermentation.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Fermentation makes ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide bubbles make the dough rise.
B: Incorrect — Yeast uses oxygen if there is any; it doesn't make it.
C: Incorrect — Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration in muscles, not yeast.
D: Incorrect — The dough rises before baking, because of carbon dioxide from fermentation.

questions.stem: Why does your heart rate increase during exercise?
options: To cool the muscles down
To get more oxygenated blood to the muscles for respiration
To carry lactic acid into the muscles
To make the muscles photosynthesise
questions.hint: Think about what working muscles need more of.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blood does carry heat, but the main reason is to supply oxygen for respiration.
B: Correct — Muscles respire faster during exercise, so they need more oxygen and glucose and must lose more carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — Lactic acid is made in the muscles, and blood carries it away.
D: Incorrect — Animal cells can't photosynthesise.

questions.stem: During a long sprint, a runner's leg muscles ache and stop contracting properly. What is the cause?
options: The heart has stopped pumping blood to the legs
The muscles have made too much ethanol
The muscles have run out of carbon dioxide
Not enough oxygen, so the muscles respire anaerobically and lactic acid builds up
questions.hint: The muscles can't get oxygen fast enough.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The heart pumps harder during exercise, not less.
B: Incorrect — Human muscles make lactic acid, not ethanol.
C: Incorrect — Muscles don't need carbon dioxide. They give it out.
D: Correct — Lactic acid builds up and the muscles become fatigued, so they stop contracting efficiently.

questions.stem: Which molecules join together to make a lipid (fat) molecule?
options: Many glucose molecules
Many amino acids
One glucose and three amino acids
One glycerol and three fatty acids
questions.hint: There are two kinds of molecule, in a 1 : 3 ratio.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glucose molecules join to make starch, glycogen or cellulose.
B: Incorrect — Amino acids join to make proteins.
C: Incorrect — This doesn't describe how any molecule in the spec is made.
D: Correct — Lipids are made from one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid molecules.

questions.stem: Which of these is a use of the energy transferred by respiration?
options: Keeping warm
Absorbing light in leaves
Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water
Making oxygen in the lungs
questions.hint: Respiration supplies energy for living processes in the body.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Organisms use energy from respiration for keeping warm, movement and building larger molecules.
B: Incorrect — Light is absorbed by chlorophyll. It doesn't need energy from respiration.
C: Incorrect — That is photosynthesis, which uses light energy.
D: Incorrect — The lungs don't make oxygen. They take it in from the air.

questions.stem: After hard exercise, what happens to the lactic acid in the muscles?
options: The kidneys excrete all of it straight away in urine
It is breathed out of the lungs as lactic acid
It stays in the muscles and is stored as glycogen
Blood carries it to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose
questions.hint: Blood carries it to a large organ that deals with many chemicals.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The liver deals with lactic acid by turning it back into glucose.
B: Incorrect — Lactic acid is not a gas and is not breathed out.
C: Incorrect — Blood carries the lactic acid away to the liver.
D: Correct — This needs extra oxygen, which is why you keep breathing hard after exercise.

questions.stem: Why do you keep breathing deeply for several minutes after a hard race?
options: To cool the lungs down after the race
To repay the oxygen debt: the extra oxygen needed to react with the lactic acid and remove it
To breathe out the lactic acid
To take in more carbon dioxide for the muscles
questions.hint: The body needs to deal with something that built up during the race.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The main reason is to supply extra oxygen, not to cool the lungs.
B: Correct — Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to remove the lactic acid that built up.
C: Incorrect — Lactic acid isn't breathed out. It is broken down using oxygen.
D: Incorrect — The body gets rid of carbon dioxide. It doesn't need to take it in.

questions.stem: A plant's roots are in waterlogged soil with no oxygen. The root cells respire anaerobically. What do they make?
options: Lactic acid
Ethanol and carbon dioxide
Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
questions.hint: Plant cells respire anaerobically in the same way as yeast.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration in animal muscles, not plants.
B: Correct — Anaerobic respiration in plant cells and yeast is glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
C: Incorrect — These are made by photosynthesis, not respiration.
D: Incorrect — These are made by aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.

questions.stem: Which of these metabolic reactions BREAKS DOWN a molecule, rather than building a larger one?
options: Amino acids join to form a protein
Glucose is turned into starch
Excess protein is broken down to form urea for excretion
Glycerol and fatty acids form a lipid
questions.hint: Three of these join small molecules together.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This builds a larger molecule from smaller ones.
B: Incorrect — This joins many glucose molecules into a larger one.
C: Correct — This is a breakdown reaction. Urea is then removed from the body.
D: Incorrect — This builds a larger molecule from smaller ones.

questions.stem: What is homeostasis?
options: Letting body conditions change to match the outside world
The breakdown of glucose to release energy
Keeping the conditions inside the body steady at the best levels
The way the body fights off pathogens
questions.hint: "Homeo" means "same" and "stasis" means "standing still".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Homeostasis stops internal conditions changing with the surroundings.
B: Incorrect — That describes respiration.
C: Correct — Homeostasis regulates internal conditions, such as temperature and blood glucose, even when things change inside or outside the body.
D: Incorrect — That describes the immune system.

questions.stem: Which of these does homeostasis control in the human body?
options: Height
Blood glucose concentration
Eye colour
The number of teeth
questions.hint: It is something that would change from minute to minute if it wasn't controlled.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Height changes slowly as you grow. It isn't kept steady by homeostasis.
B: Correct — Blood glucose, body temperature and water levels are all controlled by homeostasis.
C: Incorrect — Eye colour is set by your genes and doesn't need constant control.
D: Incorrect — The number of teeth isn't controlled by homeostasis.

questions.stem: In an automatic control system, what is an effector?
options: A cell that detects a change
The part that receives information and decides what to do
The change that sets the system off
A muscle or gland that brings about a response
questions.hint: It is the part that actually does something.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes a receptor.
B: Incorrect — That describes a coordination centre, such as the brain or pancreas.
C: Incorrect — That is the stimulus.
D: Correct — Effectors carry out the response that restores the best level.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep conditions inside the body steady?
options: So that pathogens can't get into the body
So that the body never needs to eat or drink
So that enzymes and cells work at their best
So that the body can grow taller
questions.hint: Think about the proteins that speed up reactions in cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Keeping pathogens out is the job of defences like the skin.
B: Incorrect — We still need food and water. Homeostasis controls levels, it doesn't replace them.
C: Correct — Enzymes and cells only work well in a narrow range of conditions.
D: Incorrect — Homeostasis isn't about growing taller.

questions.stem: Which of these is a coordination centre in a control system?
options: Temperature receptors in the skin
The pancreas
A sweat gland
An arm muscle
questions.hint: Coordination centres receive and process information from receptors.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Receptors detect changes. They don't coordinate the response.
B: Correct — The brain, spinal cord and pancreas are coordination centres.
C: Incorrect — A gland that responds is an effector.
D: Incorrect — A muscle that responds is an effector.

questions.stem: A student sees a ball coming towards them and catches it. Which list correctly gives the receptor, coordination centre and effector?
options: Arm muscles → brain → light receptors in the eye
Light receptors in the eye → arm muscles → brain
Brain → light receptors in the eye → arm muscles
Light receptors in the eye → brain → arm muscles
questions.hint: Follow the order: detect → decide → do.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is backwards: the muscles respond, they don't detect.
B: Incorrect — The brain must coordinate before the muscles respond.
C: Incorrect — The brain coordinates. It doesn't detect the ball.
D: Correct — The eye detects the ball, the brain coordinates and the arm muscles respond.

questions.stem: What makes up the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: All the nerves in the arms and legs
The heart and lungs
The brain and the eyes
The brain and spinal cord
questions.hint: It runs down the middle of your body.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These nerves carry impulses to and from the CNS but aren't part of it.
B: Incorrect — These are organs of the circulatory and breathing systems.
C: Incorrect — The eyes are sense organs that contain receptors.
D: Correct — The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. It coordinates the response of effectors.

questions.stem: Which neurone carries impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system?
options: Relay neurone
Sensory neurone
Effector neurone
Motor neurone
questions.hint: It carries information about what you sense.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Relay neurones are in the CNS and pass impulses from sensory to motor neurones.
B: Correct — Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.
C: Incorrect — There is no such neurone. Effectors are muscles or glands.
D: Incorrect — Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

questions.stem: Why are reflex actions important?
options: They help you make careful decisions
They are slow but last a long time
They make the body produce hormones
They are fast and automatic, so they protect the body from harm
questions.hint: Think about touching something very hot.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Reflexes skip the conscious part of the brain, so no decision is made.
B: Incorrect — Reflexes are very fast. Slow, long-lasting effects come from hormones.
C: Incorrect — Reflexes use nerves, not hormones.
D: Correct — Reflexes happen without thinking, so you react quickly to danger.

questions.stem: What is a synapse?
options: The gap where two neurones meet
The end of a muscle
A type of receptor in the skin
A hormone made by the brain
questions.hint: Neurones don't quite touch each other.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Impulses cross the synapse using a chemical.
B: Incorrect — Muscles are effectors, not synapses.
C: Incorrect — Receptors detect stimuli. A synapse is a junction between neurones.
D: Incorrect — A synapse is a gap, not a hormone.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of a reflex arc?
options: Effector → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → receptor
Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
Receptor → relay neurone → sensory neurone → motor neurone → effector
Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
questions.hint: Start with what detects the stimulus.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The receptor comes first and the effector last.
B: Correct — Information goes in by the sensory neurone, across the relay neurone and out by the motor neurone.
C: Incorrect — The sensory neurone comes before the relay neurone.
D: Incorrect — Sensory and motor neurones are the wrong way round.

questions.stem: How does a nerve impulse pass across a synapse?
options: A chemical is released, diffuses across the gap and starts an impulse in the next neurone
The two neurones join together for a moment
A hormone travels in the blood to the next neurone
The electrical impulse jumps straight across the gap
questions.hint: The impulse can't jump the gap as electricity.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The impulse is carried across the synapse by a chemical, not electrically.
B: Incorrect — The neurones don't join. There is always a gap.
C: Incorrect — Hormones work through the blood. Synapses use a chemical that diffuses across a tiny gap.
D: Incorrect — The impulse is passed on by a chemical, not electrically.

questions.stem: In a reflex arc, where is the relay neurone found?
options: In the spinal cord
In the blood
In the skin
In the muscle
questions.hint: It is part of the central nervous system, but not the thinking part of the brain.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The relay neurone in the spinal cord links the sensory and motor neurones, so the response skips conscious thought.
B: Incorrect — Neurones aren't carried in the blood.
C: Incorrect — The skin has receptors and sensory neurones, not relay neurones.
D: Incorrect — The muscle is the effector.

questions.stem: In a reaction-time test, one person drops a ruler and another catches it. What should be measured?
options: How hard the ruler is gripped
How long the ruler is
How high the ruler is held above the floor
How far the ruler falls before it is caught
questions.hint: A faster reaction means the ruler doesn't get as far.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Grip strength isn't a measure of reaction time.
B: Incorrect — The ruler's length stays the same every time.
C: Incorrect — This should be kept the same. It isn't the result.
D: Correct — A shorter distance means a faster reaction. A conversion table can turn the distance into a time.

questions.stem: Why should each person do the ruler-drop test several times?
options: So the ruler warms up
Because the first result is always wrong
So a mean can be calculated, which reduces the effect of random errors
So the person gets tired and slows down
questions.hint: One result might be a fluke.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The temperature of the ruler doesn't matter.
B: Incorrect — The first result isn't always wrong. Repeats help spot ones that are.
C: Correct — Repeating and taking a mean makes the result more reliable and helps spot anomalies.
D: Incorrect — Getting tired would change the result unfairly.

questions.stem: A student tests whether drinking cola (with caffeine) affects reaction time, using the ruler-drop test. Which is a control variable?
options: The person uses the same hand every time
Whether the person has had the cola
The reaction time
The distance the ruler falls
questions.hint: A control variable is kept the same so the test is fair.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Using the same hand keeps the test fair, so only the caffeine changes.
B: Incorrect — This is the independent variable: the one being changed on purpose.
C: Incorrect — This is what the experiment measures (the dependent variable).
D: Incorrect — This is the dependent variable: the result being measured.

questions.stem: Why is a reflex response faster than a response you think about?
options: Nerve impulses travel faster during reflexes
The impulse goes through a relay neurone in the spinal cord and skips the conscious part of the brain
Reflexes use hormones, which act faster
A reflex arc has no synapses
questions.hint: Think about which parts of the nervous system the impulse goes through.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Impulses travel at a similar speed. The pathway is shorter and skips decision-making.
B: Correct — No time is spent making a decision, so the response is automatic and rapid.
C: Incorrect — Reflexes use nerves. Hormones act more slowly.
D: Incorrect — A reflex arc does have synapses, between each neurone.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordinates muscle movement?
options: Medulla
Spinal cord
Cerebellum
Cerebral cortex
questions.hint: It is at the back of the brain, below the main folded part.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
B: Incorrect — The spinal cord is part of the CNS but isn't part of the brain.
C: Correct — The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity, such as balance.
D: Incorrect — The cerebral cortex deals with consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain controls your heartbeat and breathing without you thinking about it?
options: Cerebellum
Pituitary gland
Medulla
Cerebral cortex
questions.hint: It is at the base of the brain, joining the spinal cord.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement and balance.
B: Incorrect — The pituitary releases hormones. It doesn't control heartbeat and breathing.
C: Correct — The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
D: Incorrect — The cerebral cortex controls conscious thought, memory and language.

questions.stem: Why is it very hard to treat damage deep inside the brain?
options: The brain can't be seen with any scanner
Brain cells are all the same, so you can't tell where the damage is
The brain has no blood supply
The brain is complex and delicate, so treatment can damage other areas
questions.hint: Think about what surgery might hit on the way in.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — MRI scans can show the brain. That is how scientists mapped its regions.
B: Incorrect — Different regions of the brain have different jobs.
C: Incorrect — The brain has a large blood supply.
D: Correct — It is hard to reach one region without harming others, and we still don't fully understand how the brain works.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye contains receptor cells that are sensitive to light?
options: Retina
Cornea
Sclera
Iris
questions.hint: It is at the back of the eye.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The retina has light receptors, which send impulses along the optic nerve to the brain.
B: Incorrect — The cornea is the clear front of the eye that bends light as it enters.
C: Incorrect — The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye.
D: Incorrect — The iris controls how much light enters through the pupil.

questions.stem: You walk into a dark room. How does your eye let in more light?
options: The cornea becomes clearer
The iris makes the pupil wider
The lens gets thicker
The iris makes the pupil smaller
questions.hint: Look at the black hole in the middle of the eye.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The cornea is always clear. It doesn't change in the dark.
B: Correct — A wider pupil lets more light reach the retina.
C: Incorrect — Lens shape changes to focus light, not to let in more of it.
D: Incorrect — A smaller pupil lets less light in. That happens in bright light.

questions.stem: What happens in the eye when you focus on a book close to your face?
options: The pupil closes completely
Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments tighten, the lens gets thinner
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments loosen, the lens gets thicker and bends light more
The retina moves closer to the lens
questions.hint: To focus on something near, light needs to be bent more.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The pupil never closes completely, and that wouldn't focus the light.
B: Incorrect — This happens when you look at something far away.
C: Correct — A thicker lens refracts light more strongly, which is needed for near objects.
D: Incorrect — The retina stays in place. The lens changes shape instead.

questions.stem: A short-sighted person (myopia) can't see distant objects clearly. Which statement is correct?
options: Light is focused in front of the retina; a concave lens corrects it
The retina has no light receptors; a lens can't help
Light is focused in front of the retina; a convex lens corrects it
Light is focused behind the retina; a convex lens corrects it
questions.hint: In myopia the light is bent too much.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — A concave lens spreads light out a little, so it focuses on the retina.
B: Incorrect — Short-sighted people have working retinas. Glasses, contact lenses or laser surgery can help.
C: Incorrect — A convex lens would bend light even more and make it worse.
D: Incorrect — This describes long-sightedness (hyperopia).

questions.stem: A long-sighted person (hyperopia) can't see near objects clearly. Where does the light focus, and which lens corrects it?
options: On the retina; no lens is needed
Behind the retina; a convex lens
Behind the retina; a concave lens
In front of the retina; a concave lens
questions.hint: In hyperopia the light isn't bent enough.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — If the light focused on the retina, the person would see clearly.
B: Correct — A convex lens bends light more, bringing the focus forward onto the retina.
C: Incorrect — A concave lens spreads light out, which would make the focus fall even further back.
D: Incorrect — This describes short-sightedness (myopia).

questions.stem: Which part of the body monitors and controls body temperature?
options: The pancreas
The thermoregulatory centre in the brain
The heart
The skin alone
questions.hint: It has receptors that check the temperature of the blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The pancreas controls blood glucose.
B: Correct — It contains receptors sensitive to blood temperature and gets impulses from receptors in the skin.
C: Incorrect — The heart pumps blood. It doesn't control body temperature.
D: Incorrect — Skin has temperature receptors, but the brain coordinates the response.

questions.stem: How does the body respond when its temperature rises too high?
options: Blood vessels to the skin widen (vasodilation) and more sweat is made
The heart stops pumping blood to the skin
Sweating stops and the muscles shiver
Blood vessels to the skin narrow (vasoconstriction) and shivering starts
questions.hint: You go red and damp on a hot day.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — More blood near the skin and evaporating sweat both transfer energy away from the body.
B: Incorrect — Blood still flows to the skin. More of it flows near the surface when you are hot.
C: Incorrect — These responses warm the body up.
D: Incorrect — This is how the body responds to being too cold.

questions.stem: A walker gets very cold and starts to shiver. How does shivering raise body temperature?
options: Shivering widens blood vessels in the skin
Muscles contract quickly, so they respire more, and respiration transfers energy that warms the body
Shivering stops respiration, so less energy is lost
Shivering makes sweat, which warms the skin
questions.hint: Think about what muscles need to contract, and what that process gives out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Widening blood vessels near the skin loses heat. When cold, they narrow.
B: Correct — Respiration is exothermic, so the extra respiration in shivering muscles warms the body.
C: Incorrect — Shivering increases respiration in the muscles.
D: Incorrect — Sweating cools the body, and it stops when you are cold.

questions.stem: How are hormones carried to their target organs?
options: In the bloodstream
Along nerves as electrical impulses
Through the digestive system
Through the air we breathe out
questions.hint: They are released by glands straight into a liquid that flows around the body.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Glands secrete hormones into the blood, which carries them to target organs.
B: Incorrect — Nerves carry electrical impulses. Hormones are chemicals in the blood.
C: Incorrect — Hormones travel in the blood, not through the gut.
D: Incorrect — Hormones stay inside the body.

questions.stem: Which gland is called the "master gland"?
options: The thyroid gland
The adrenal gland
The pituitary gland
The pancreas
questions.hint: It is in the brain and controls other glands.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The thyroid makes thyroxine. It is controlled by the pituitary.
B: Incorrect — The adrenal glands make adrenaline.
C: Correct — It releases hormones that make other glands release their hormones.
D: Incorrect — The pancreas makes insulin to control blood glucose.

questions.stem: How do the effects of hormones compare with the effects of the nervous system?
options: Hormones act more slowly but their effects last longer
Hormones and nerves act at exactly the same speed
Hormones act faster and their effects are shorter
Hormones only work on the brain
questions.hint: Hormones have to travel in the blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Hormones take time to travel in the blood, but they act for longer.
B: Incorrect — Nerve impulses are much faster than hormones.
C: Incorrect — Nervous responses are the fast, short ones.
D: Incorrect — Hormones act on target organs all over the body.

questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises. Which hormone brings it back down?
options: Adrenaline
Oestrogen
Insulin
Testosterone
questions.hint: People with type 1 diabetes need to inject it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Adrenaline prepares the body for "fight or flight".
B: Incorrect — Oestrogen is a female reproductive hormone.
C: Correct — The pancreas releases insulin, which makes glucose move from the blood into cells.
D: Incorrect — Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone.

questions.stem: Insulin makes liver and muscle cells store extra glucose. What is it stored as?
options: Starch
Glycogen
Urea
Glucagon
questions.hint: Animals and plants store glucose differently.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Starch is how plants store glucose.
B: Correct — In liver and muscle cells, excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
C: Incorrect — Urea is a waste product made from excess protein.
D: Incorrect — Glucagon is a hormone, not a store of glucose.

questions.stem: What causes type 1 diabetes, and how is it treated?
options: The pancreas makes too much insulin; it is treated with antibiotics
Body cells stop responding to insulin; it is treated with diet and exercise
The kidneys stop working; it is treated with dialysis
The pancreas makes too little insulin; it is treated with insulin injections
questions.hint: In type 1, the problem is with the organ that makes insulin.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Type 1 is too little insulin, and antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
B: Incorrect — This describes type 2 diabetes.
C: Incorrect — That describes kidney failure.
D: Correct — Without enough insulin, blood glucose can rise dangerously high.

questions.stem: Which statement about type 2 diabetes is correct?
options: It is caused by a virus and can be cured with antibiotics
The pancreas stops making insulin, and it is usually treated with insulin injections
Body cells stop responding to insulin; obesity is a risk factor
It makes blood glucose fall too low
questions.hint: In type 2, insulin is still made.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Diabetes isn't caused by a pathogen, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.
B: Incorrect — This describes type 1 diabetes.
C: Correct — It is treated with a carbohydrate-controlled diet and exercise.
D: Incorrect — Diabetes makes blood glucose too high.

questions.stem: A person has not eaten for many hours and their blood glucose falls. What happens next?
options: The pancreas releases more insulin to raise blood glucose
The kidneys release glucose from the urine back into the blood
The liver turns glucose into glycogen
The pancreas releases glucagon, which makes the liver turn glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood
questions.hint: The pancreas makes a second hormone that does the opposite of insulin.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Insulin lowers blood glucose, so more insulin would make it worse.
B: Incorrect — Glucose is raised by glucagon acting on the liver.
C: Incorrect — That lowers blood glucose. It happens when glucose is too high.
D: Correct — Glucagon raises blood glucose. Insulin and glucagon work together in a negative feedback cycle.

questions.stem: Two people have a sugary drink. In person A, blood glucose rises then falls back to normal within 2 hours. In person B, it rises higher and stays high. What is the most likely reason?
options: Person B makes too much insulin
Person B's liver turns too much glycogen into glucose
Person A has diabetes
Person B has type 1 diabetes and makes too little insulin, so glucose isn't moved into cells
questions.hint: Think about which hormone moves glucose out of the blood.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Too much insulin would make blood glucose fall, not stay high.
B: Incorrect — The problem is glucose not being taken out of the blood, which is insulin's job.
C: Incorrect — Person A's glucose returns to normal, which is what happens without diabetes.
D: Correct — Without enough insulin, glucose stays in the blood for much longer.

questions.stem: What is the main female reproductive hormone, made in the ovaries?
options: Testosterone
Adrenaline
Insulin
Oestrogen
questions.hint: It also starts the development of female features at puberty.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone, made in the testes.
B: Incorrect — Adrenaline is released in times of fear or stress.
C: Incorrect — Insulin controls blood glucose.
D: Correct — At puberty, oestrogen causes eggs to begin maturing and female secondary sex characteristics to develop.

questions.stem: What do FSH and LH do in the menstrual cycle?
options: FSH causes the egg to be released; LH makes an egg mature
Both stop sperm being made
FSH makes an egg mature in the ovary; LH causes the egg to be released
Both keep the lining of the uterus thick
questions.hint: One gets the egg ready; the other lets it go.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are the wrong way round.
B: Incorrect — FSH and LH control the egg in the menstrual cycle.
C: Correct — LH triggers ovulation, which happens about every 28 days.
D: Incorrect — Oestrogen and progesterone maintain the uterus lining.

questions.stem: In the menstrual cycle, what effect does a rising level of oestrogen have on FSH and LH?
options: It stops FSH being released and makes LH be released
It stops both FSH and LH
It makes more FSH and stops LH
It has no effect on either hormone
questions.hint: Once an egg is maturing, the body doesn't need more eggs maturing, but it does need one released.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This stops more eggs maturing and triggers ovulation.
B: Incorrect — Progesterone stops both. Oestrogen stimulates LH.
C: Incorrect — This is the opposite of what happens.
D: Incorrect — The hormones of the cycle affect each other.

questions.stem: How does a condom help prevent pregnancy?
options: It releases hormones that stop eggs maturing
It stops an embryo implanting in the uterus
It kills the egg
It stops sperm reaching an egg
questions.hint: It is a barrier method.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes hormonal methods such as the pill or an implant.
B: Incorrect — That is how some IUDs (coils) work.
C: Incorrect — Condoms don't affect eggs. They block sperm.
D: Correct — Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms physically block sperm.

questions.stem: How does the oral contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
options: Its hormones stop FSH being made, so no eggs mature
It kills sperm in the stomach
It makes more FSH, so eggs are released too early
It forms a barrier that blocks sperm
questions.hint: It contains hormones that affect the menstrual cycle.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — No mature egg means no egg can be fertilised.
B: Incorrect — The pill is a hormone method. Sperm never reach the stomach.
C: Incorrect — The pill stops FSH, not increases it.
D: Incorrect — That is how a condom or diaphragm works.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the main steps in IVF?
options: Eggs collected → FSH and LH given → embryos put into the uterus → eggs fertilised
Eggs fertilised in the woman's body → eggs collected → FSH and LH given
FSH and LH given → eggs collected → eggs fertilised in a lab → one or two embryos put into the uterus
Embryos put into the uterus → FSH and LH given → eggs collected
questions.hint: The eggs must mature before they can be collected.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Eggs are fertilised in the lab before going into the uterus.
B: Incorrect — In IVF fertilisation happens in the lab.
C: Correct — The hormones make several eggs mature. Fertilised eggs grow into tiny balls of cells before being inserted.
D: Incorrect — Embryos can't be made until eggs have been collected and fertilised.

questions.stem: Someone gets a sudden fright. Their adrenal glands release adrenaline. What does adrenaline do?
options: Increases heart rate, sending more oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles
Lowers blood glucose by moving it into cells
Makes eggs mature in the ovary
Lowers heart rate so the body can relax
questions.hint: It gets the body ready for "fight or flight".
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This prepares the body to fight or run away.
B: Incorrect — That is what insulin does.
C: Incorrect — That is the job of FSH.
D: Incorrect — Adrenaline increases heart rate.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland releases thyroxine, which raises the basal metabolic rate. If the thyroxine level in the blood gets too high, what happens?
options: Nothing happens until thyroxine runs out
The thyroid makes even more thyroxine
The pancreas releases glucagon to lower the thyroxine
The pituitary releases less of the hormone that stimulates the thyroid, so less thyroxine is made
questions.hint: Thyroxine is controlled by negative feedback.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The level is controlled all the time by negative feedback.
B: Incorrect — That would make the level rise further. That is the opposite of negative feedback.
C: Incorrect — Glucagon raises blood glucose. It doesn't control thyroxine.
D: Correct — Negative feedback: a rise causes a response that brings the level back down.

questions.stem: Through which of these does the body lose water without being able to control the amount?
options: The heart, in blood
The lungs, when we breathe out
The kidneys, in urine
The pancreas, in insulin
questions.hint: Think about what happens every time you breathe out.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blood stays in the circulatory system.
B: Correct — Water is lost from the lungs in exhaled air, and the body doesn't control how much.
C: Incorrect — The kidneys do control how much water is lost in urine.
D: Incorrect — The pancreas doesn't remove water from the body.

questions.stem: Glucose is filtered out of the blood in the kidneys, but a healthy person's urine has no glucose in it. Why?
options: The glucose is turned into urea
The bladder uses up the glucose
Glucose is too big to be filtered
All the glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood (selective reabsorption)
questions.hint: Useful substances are taken back.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Urea is made from excess amino acids, not glucose.
B: Incorrect — All of it is reabsorbed in the kidneys before urine reaches the bladder.
C: Incorrect — Glucose is filtered out of the blood. It is then reabsorbed.
D: Correct — The kidneys filter the blood, then take back useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water.

questions.stem: In kidney dialysis, why does the dialysis fluid contain no urea?
options: To make the blood take in more water
So urea diffuses out of the blood into the fluid, down a concentration gradient
Because urea would block the partially permeable membrane
So urea moves from the fluid into the blood
questions.hint: Substances diffuse from high concentration to low concentration.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Dialysis is mainly about removing waste such as urea, not adding water to the blood.
B: Correct — The fluid has the same glucose and useful ions as normal blood, so only waste like urea leaves.
C: Incorrect — The point is to make urea leave by diffusion.
D: Incorrect — Urea is a waste product. The aim is to remove it from the blood.

questions.stem: After a long run without drinking, the blood becomes too concentrated. How does ADH help?
options: ADH turns urea into water
More ADH is released, making the kidney tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood
Less ADH is released, so more water leaves in urine
ADH makes the person sweat more
questions.hint: ADH is released by the pituitary and acts on the kidney tubules.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed. It doesn't change urea.
B: Correct — Less, more concentrated urine is made. This is controlled by negative feedback.
C: Incorrect — That happens when the blood is too dilute.
D: Incorrect — ADH acts on the kidney tubules, not the sweat glands.

questions.stem: What happens to excess amino acids from protein in the diet?
options: They are stored in the liver as glycogen
The liver deaminates them to make ammonia, which is quickly turned into less toxic urea
They are breathed out as ammonia
They are turned into glucose by insulin
questions.hint: The liver removes the part containing nitrogen.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Glycogen is a store of glucose, not amino acids.
B: Correct — Ammonia is toxic, so it is converted to urea, which the kidneys excrete.
C: Incorrect — Ammonia is turned into urea and removed in urine.
D: Incorrect — Insulin moves glucose into cells. It doesn't act on amino acids.

questions.stem: What is phototropism?
options: The loss of water from leaves
The process of making glucose using light
A plant's growth response to light
A plant's growth response to gravity
questions.hint: "Photo" means light.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is transpiration.
B: Incorrect — That is photosynthesis.
C: Correct — Shoots grow towards light, which helps them photosynthesise.
D: Incorrect — That is gravitropism (also called geotropism).

questions.stem: Which plant hormone controls the growth of shoots towards light?
options: Auxin
Ethene
Insulin
Chlorophyll
questions.hint: It is found in shoot and root tips.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — An unequal spread of auxin causes unequal growth, so the shoot bends.
B: Incorrect — Ethene controls cell division and fruit ripening.
C: Incorrect — Insulin is a human hormone that controls blood glucose.
D: Incorrect — Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis. It isn't a hormone.

questions.stem: Light shines on a shoot from one side only. Why does the shoot bend towards the light?
options: Auxin builds up on the lit side, so cells there grow faster
Auxin builds up on the shaded side, so cells there grow longer faster
The shoot has muscles that pull it round
Light kills cells on the lit side
questions.hint: Think about which side ends up with more auxin.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — More auxin on the lit side would bend the shoot away from the light.
B: Correct — The shaded side grows more, which bends the shoot towards the light.
C: Incorrect — Plants don't have muscles. They respond by growing.
D: Incorrect — Light doesn't kill the cells. Unequal auxin causes unequal growth.

questions.stem: A seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Its root bends and grows downwards. Why?
options: Auxin collects on the lower side, where it slows root growth, so the root bends down
Ethene makes the root fall down
Auxin collects on the lower side, where it speeds up root growth
The root is growing towards light
questions.hint: Auxin has the opposite effect in roots compared with shoots.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — In roots, auxin slows growth, so the upper side grows more and the root curves downwards.
B: Incorrect — Ethene controls cell division and ripening, not gravitropism.
C: Incorrect — If the lower side grew faster, the root would bend upwards.
D: Incorrect — The seedling is in the dark. The root is responding to gravity.

questions.stem: A student grows cress seedlings in three dishes with light from different directions. Why should every dish have the same type of seed and the same amount of water?
options: So the seedlings grow faster
So the seedlings all bend the same way
So that only the direction of light affects how the seedlings grow
So the student doesn't need to measure the seedlings
questions.hint: Only one thing should change between dishes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The aim is a fair test, not faster growth.
B: Incorrect — The student wants to see if the direction of light changes how they bend.
C: Correct — Keeping control variables the same makes it a fair test.
D: Incorrect — Lengths still need measuring and recording.

questions.stem: A supermarket wants bananas picked unripe to ripen just before they go on sale. Which plant hormone is used?
options: Gibberellin
Insulin
Auxin
Ethene
questions.hint: It is a gas that controls fruit ripening.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gibberellins end seed dormancy, promote flowering and increase fruit size.
B: Incorrect — Insulin is a human hormone.
C: Incorrect — Auxins are used in weedkillers and rooting powders.
D: Correct — Ethene is used to control ripening during storage and transport.

questions.stem: A grower has dormant seeds and wants them all to start germinating. Which hormone should they use?
options: Ethene
Adrenaline
Gibberellin
Auxin
questions.hint: This hormone is important in starting germination.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Ethene controls ripening of fruits.
B: Incorrect — Adrenaline is a human hormone.
C: Correct — Gibberellins start seed germination and are used to end seed dormancy.
D: Incorrect — Auxins are used as weedkillers, in rooting powders and in tissue culture.

questions.stem: What are the gametes in flowering plants?
options: Seeds and fruits
Sperm and egg cells
Pollen and egg cells
Root hair cells and leaf cells
questions.hint: One of them is carried by insects or the wind.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Seeds and fruits form after fertilisation. They aren't gametes.
B: Incorrect — These are the gametes in animals.
C: Correct — In flowering plants the male gamete is in the pollen and the female gamete is the egg cell.
D: Incorrect — These are body cells, not sex cells.

questions.stem: How many parents are involved in asexual reproduction?
options: Four
None
One
Two
questions.hint: "A-" at the start of a word often means "without".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — No type of reproduction needs four parents.
B: Incorrect — Every new organism comes from at least one parent.
C: Correct — Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no joining of gametes.
D: Incorrect — Two parents are needed for sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: What is true about the offspring made by asexual reproduction?
options: They are all genetically different
They are genetically identical to the parent (clones)
They have half the parent's chromosomes
They get half their genes from each of two parents
questions.hint: There is no mixing of genetic information.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Genetic differences come from sexual reproduction.
B: Correct — Only mitosis is involved, so the offspring have exactly the same genes as the parent.
C: Incorrect — Only gametes have half the chromosomes. Asexual offspring have the full set.
D: Incorrect — That happens in sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: Why do offspring from sexual reproduction show variety?
options: The gametes are identical to each other
Only one parent passes on its genes
Genetic information from two parents is mixed
The offspring are made by mitosis only
questions.hint: Think about where their genetic information comes from.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gametes are all genetically different from each other.
B: Incorrect — One parent and no mixing is asexual reproduction, which gives clones.
C: Correct — Each gamete carries a different mix of genes, and two gametes from two parents join.
D: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical cells, so it wouldn't cause variety.

questions.stem: Which statement about meiosis and mitosis is correct?
options: Meiosis makes non-identical cells; mitosis makes identical cells
Both make identical cells
Both make gametes
Meiosis makes identical cells; mitosis makes non-identical cells
questions.hint: One makes body cells, the other makes sex cells.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Meiosis forms gametes that are all different. Mitosis makes copies for growth and repair.
B: Incorrect — Meiosis makes cells that are genetically different.
C: Incorrect — Only meiosis makes gametes.
D: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Which type of cell division makes gametes?
options: Mitosis
Meiosis
Fertilisation
Differentiation
questions.hint: It happens in the reproductive organs, such as the ovaries and testes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Mitosis makes identical body cells for growth and repair.
B: Correct — Cells in reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes.
C: Incorrect — Fertilisation is when two gametes join, not a type of division.
D: Incorrect — Differentiation is when a cell becomes specialised.

questions.stem: A cat's body cells have 38 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a cat sperm cell?
questions.hint: Gametes have a single set of chromosomes.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Meiosis halves the number of chromosomes, so each gamete has 38 ÷ 2 = 19.
B: Incorrect — Doubling the number would happen if the cell copied its chromosomes but didn't divide.
C: Incorrect — 38 is the number in body cells, not gametes.
D: Incorrect — 23 is the number in a human gamete.

questions.stem: When one cell divides by meiosis, what is produced?
options: One gamete with a double set of chromosomes
Two identical body cells
Four gametes, each genetically different
Four identical gametes
questions.hint: The cell divides twice.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Gametes have a single set, and four are made.
B: Incorrect — This describes mitosis.
C: Correct — The cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all different.
D: Incorrect — The four gametes are all genetically different from each other.

questions.stem: Why is it important that gametes have only half the normal number of chromosomes?
options: So that the offspring are clones of one parent
So that gametes can move faster
So that fertilisation restores the normal number of chromosomes
So that the embryo divides by meiosis
questions.hint: Think about what happens when two gametes join.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Offspring from fertilisation get genes from both parents, so they aren't clones.
B: Incorrect — The number of chromosomes doesn't control how fast a gamete moves.
C: Correct — Two half sets join to make one full set, so the number stays the same each generation.
D: Incorrect — After fertilisation the new cell divides by mitosis.

questions.stem: What happens straight after an egg cell is fertilised?
options: The chromosome number halves
The new cell divides by mitosis, and later the cells differentiate
The cells stop dividing
The new cell divides by meiosis to make more gametes
questions.hint: The embryo needs many identical cells to grow.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Fertilisation restores the full number. It doesn't halve it.
B: Correct — Mitosis increases the number of cells. As the embryo develops, cells become specialised.
C: Incorrect — The embryo grows because its cells keep dividing.
D: Incorrect — Meiosis only happens in reproductive organs to make gametes.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of asexual reproduction?
options: Only one parent is needed, so no time or energy is spent finding a mate
It speeds up natural selection
It produces lots of variation
The offspring are better at surviving a change in the environment
questions.hint: Think about what the organism doesn't have to do.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Asexual reproduction is faster and more efficient because no mate is needed.
B: Incorrect — Natural selection needs variation, which comes from sexual reproduction.
C: Incorrect — Asexual reproduction makes clones, so there is no variation.
D: Incorrect — Without variation, a change could kill all the identical offspring.

questions.stem: Why does sexual reproduction help a species survive if the environment changes?
options: Only one parent is needed
It makes many identical offspring
It is faster than asexual reproduction
It produces variation, so some individuals may survive the change
questions.hint: Not all the offspring are the same.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sexual reproduction needs two parents.
B: Incorrect — Identical offspring would all be affected in the same way.
C: Incorrect — Sexual reproduction is slower, not faster.
D: Correct — With variation, some offspring may have features that suit the new conditions. Natural selection favours them.

questions.stem: Strawberry plants make seeds, and they also grow new plants from runners. What type of reproduction is growing from runners?
options: Asexual, so the new plants have half the chromosomes
Asexual, so the new plants are clones
Sexual, so the new plants show variation
Sexual, because pollen is needed
questions.hint: A runner grows out from just one parent plant.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Asexual offspring have the full set of chromosomes.
B: Correct — Runners come from one parent with no gametes, so the new plants are genetically identical.
C: Incorrect — Seeds come from sexual reproduction. Runners don't.
D: Incorrect — Runners don't need pollen.

questions.stem: How do malarial parasites reproduce?
options: Only sexually, by making spores
Asexually in the human host and sexually in the mosquito
Sexually in the human host and asexually in the mosquito
Only asexually, in both hosts
questions.hint: They use different methods in their two different hosts.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Spores are used by fungi for asexual reproduction.
B: Correct — Malarial parasites use both methods, depending on where they are.
C: Incorrect — This is the wrong way round.
D: Incorrect — They also reproduce sexually in the mosquito.

questions.stem: What is a gene?
options: All the genetic material of an organism
A whole chromosome
A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a protein
A type of sex cell
questions.hint: It is part of something bigger that is found in the nucleus.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the genome.
B: Incorrect — A chromosome contains many genes.
C: Correct — Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
D: Incorrect — Sex cells are gametes.

questions.stem: Which describes the structure of DNA?
options: A short chain of amino acids
A single straight strand
A ring of four strands
A polymer of two strands twisted into a double helix
questions.hint: Picture a twisted ladder.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A chain of amino acids is a protein.
B: Incorrect — DNA has two strands, twisted together.
C: Incorrect — DNA has two strands.
D: Correct — DNA is a polymer made of two strands that form a double helix.

questions.stem: What is a genome?
options: The entire genetic material of an organism
The characteristics you can see
One section of DNA that codes for a protein
One of the two forms of a gene
questions.hint: It is the biggest of these: gene, chromosome or genome.
