questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The genome is all of an organism's DNA.
B: Incorrect — That is the phenotype.
C: Incorrect — That is a gene.
D: Incorrect — That is an allele.

questions.stem: Which of these is a use of understanding the human genome?
options: Tracing how humans migrated in the past
Making all humans genetically identical
Stopping all mutations from happening
Proving that diseases are never inherited
questions.hint: It is about medicine and about history.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Studying the genome helps trace migration patterns, find genes linked to disease and treat inherited disorders.
B: Incorrect — That isn't possible or a use of the genome project.
C: Incorrect — Mutations happen continuously. We can't stop them.
D: Incorrect — Some disorders are inherited, and the genome helps us understand them.

questions.stem: Which four bases are found in DNA?
options: A, C, G and T
A, C, G and U
X, Y, A and T
A, B, C and D
questions.hint: They are known by single letters.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — DNA contains four bases: A, C, G and T.
B: Incorrect — U isn't found in DNA.
C: Incorrect — X and Y are sex chromosomes, not bases.
D: Incorrect — These aren't the letters used for DNA bases.

questions.stem: What does a sequence of three bases in DNA code for?
options: One chromosome
One whole protein
One nucleotide
One particular amino acid
questions.hint: Proteins are built from small units joined together.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A chromosome is made of a huge length of DNA.
B: Incorrect — A protein needs many groups of three bases.
C: Incorrect — A nucleotide is one unit of DNA. It holds only one base.
D: Correct — Each group of three bases codes for one amino acid.

questions.stem: What is one nucleotide of DNA made of?
options: A chromosome and a gene
Two bases and an amino acid
Four bases joined in a ring
A sugar, a phosphate group and one base
questions.hint: DNA's backbone alternates between two parts.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are much bigger structures made of DNA.
B: Incorrect — Nucleotides don't contain amino acids.
C: Incorrect — Each nucleotide has only one base.
D: Correct — Each nucleotide has a common sugar and phosphate, with one of four bases attached to the sugar.

questions.stem: What controls the order in which amino acids are joined to make a protein?
options: The size of the nucleus
The order of bases in the DNA
The amount of sugar in the DNA
The number of chromosomes in the cell
questions.hint: Think of DNA as a code written in letters.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The nucleus size doesn't control protein structure.
B: Correct — The base sequence sets which amino acids are added, and in what order.
C: Incorrect — Every nucleotide has the same sugar, so it can't carry the code.
D: Incorrect — The chromosome number doesn't set the order of amino acids.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA has the bases A T G C. What are the bases on the matching (complementary) strand?
options: C G T A
T A C G
A T G C
G C A T
questions.hint: C always pairs with G, and T always pairs with A.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is the strand read backwards.
B: Correct — A pairs with T, T with A, G with C, and C with G.
C: Incorrect — This is the same strand, not the complementary one.
D: Incorrect — This pairs A with G, which doesn't happen.

questions.stem: Where are proteins made in a cell, and how do the right amino acids get there?
options: In the cell membrane; enzymes make amino acids from glucose
In the nucleus; the DNA itself joins the amino acids
On ribosomes; carrier molecules bring specific amino acids in the correct order
In mitochondria; amino acids diffuse in randomly
questions.hint: They are tiny structures in the cytoplasm.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Proteins aren't made in the cell membrane.
B: Incorrect — DNA holds the code, but proteins are made on ribosomes.
C: Correct — Proteins are made on ribosomes using a template. Carrier molecules bring the amino acids.
D: Incorrect — Mitochondria release energy. The order of amino acids isn't random.

questions.stem: A mutation changes the shape of an enzyme's active site. What is the most likely effect?
options: The substrate no longer fits, so the enzyme doesn't work properly
The enzyme turns into a carbohydrate
The enzyme works faster
Nothing, because enzymes don't depend on shape
questions.hint: Think about lock and key.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — An altered protein shape means the enzyme may no longer fit its substrate.
B: Incorrect — A mutation changes the protein. It doesn't turn it into something else.
C: Incorrect — A changed active site usually stops the substrate fitting.
D: Incorrect — An enzyme's shape is what lets it do its job.

questions.stem: Most mutations have no effect on an organism. Why?
options: They don't change the protein, or change it so slightly that it still works the same
The body repairs every mutation straight away
Mutations only change the sugar in DNA
Mutations only happen in dead cells
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the protein.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Most mutations don't alter the protein, or only alter it a little, so its appearance or function isn't changed.
B: Incorrect — Not every mutation is repaired.
C: Incorrect — Mutations change the base sequence.
D: Incorrect — Mutations happen continuously in living cells.

questions.stem: Some DNA doesn't code for proteins. How can a change in this non-coding DNA affect an organism?
options: It can't have any effect at all
It changes the amino acids in every protein
It can change whether genes are switched on or off
It changes the number of chromosomes
questions.hint: Non-coding DNA works like a set of switches.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Non-coding DNA controls gene expression, so changes can matter.
B: Incorrect — Non-coding DNA doesn't code for amino acids.
C: Correct — Non-coding DNA can switch genes on and off, so variants here change how genes are expressed.
D: Incorrect — A change in the base sequence doesn't change the chromosome number.

questions.stem: What is an allele?
options: A different form of a gene
A sex cell
A whole set of chromosomes
A characteristic you can see
questions.hint: Eye colour has one gene but more than one version.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Each gene may have different forms called alleles.
B: Incorrect — A sex cell is a gamete.
C: Incorrect — A set of chromosomes holds thousands of genes.
D: Incorrect — That is part of the phenotype.

questions.stem: An organism has the genotype Bb. What is it?
options: Homozygous recessive
A phenotype
Homozygous dominant
Heterozygous
questions.hint: Look at whether the two letters are the same.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Homozygous recessive would be bb.
B: Incorrect — Bb is a genotype: the alleles present.
C: Incorrect — Homozygous dominant would be BB.
D: Correct — The two alleles are different, so it is heterozygous.

questions.stem: What does "phenotype" mean?
options: The alleles an organism has
Having two identical alleles
A small section of DNA
The characteristics that are expressed, such as fur colour
questions.hint: "Pheno" comes from a word meaning "to show".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is the genotype.
B: Incorrect — That is homozygous.
C: Incorrect — That is a gene.
D: Correct — The phenotype is what develops from the alleles present.

questions.stem: When is a recessive allele expressed?
options: Whenever one copy is present
Never
Only when two copies are present
Only in gametes
questions.hint: A dominant allele always wins if it is there.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That describes a dominant allele.
B: Incorrect — Recessive alleles are expressed when two copies are present.
C: Correct — A recessive allele is only expressed if there is no dominant allele.
D: Incorrect — Alleles are expressed in the organism, not just in gametes.

questions.stem: In mice, the allele for brown fur (B) is dominant to the allele for white fur (b). What colour is a mouse with genotype Bb?
options: Half brown, half white
White
Light brown
Brown
questions.hint: Only one copy of a dominant allele is needed.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The alleles don't mix like this. B is dominant.
B: Incorrect — White fur needs two recessive alleles, bb.
C: Incorrect — In this cross B is fully dominant, so there is no blending.
D: Correct — The dominant allele B is expressed even with only one copy.

questions.stem: A Punnett square for a cross between Bb and bb mice gives these offspring: Bb, Bb, bb, bb. White fur is recessive. What proportion of offspring are expected to be white?
questions.hint: Count how many have two recessive alleles.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That would be 1 bb out of 4.
B: Incorrect — The Bb offspring would be brown.
C: Correct — 2 out of 4 offspring are bb, so half are expected to be white.
D: Incorrect — Only two of the four boxes are bb.

questions.stem: Two parents are both heterozygous (Tt) for a characteristic. t is recessive. What is the probability that their child is tt?
questions.hint: Draw a 2 × 2 Punnett square with T and t from each parent.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — 75% is the chance of a child with at least one T.
B: Incorrect — Each parent carries t, so tt is possible.
C: Incorrect — 50% is the chance of a Tt child.
D: Correct — The cross gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt: 1 out of 4 is tt.

questions.stem: A plant with genotype RR is crossed with a plant with genotype rr. What proportion of the offspring are heterozygous?
questions.hint: One parent can only give R; the other can only give r.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — All the offspring are Rr, which is heterozygous.
B: Incorrect — There is no way to get RR or rr from this cross.
C: Correct — Every offspring gets R from one parent and r from the other, so all are Rr.
D: Incorrect — 25% would come from a cross between two heterozygous parents.

questions.stem: Two brown mice have a white baby. Brown (B) is dominant and white (b) is recessive. What are the parents' genotypes?
options: Bb and Bb
bb and bb
BB and BB
BB and Bb
questions.hint: The white baby must be bb. Where did each b come from?
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The baby got one b from each parent, and both parents are brown, so both must be Bb.
B: Incorrect — bb mice would be white, not brown.
C: Incorrect — BB parents can only pass on B, so a white baby couldn't happen.
D: Incorrect — The BB parent can't pass on b, so the baby couldn't be bb.

questions.stem: Which statement about how characteristics are inherited is correct?
options: Most characteristics are the result of many genes interacting
Dominant alleles are always more common than recessive ones
Characteristics are never affected by genes
Every characteristic is controlled by one gene
questions.hint: Fur colour in mice is a rare, simple example.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Only a few characteristics are controlled by a single gene. Most involve many genes.
B: Incorrect — Dominant means expressed with one copy, not more common.
C: Incorrect — Genes do affect characteristics.
D: Incorrect — Single-gene characteristics, like red-green colour blindness, are the exception.

questions.stem: What causes polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes)?
options: A bacterial infection
A recessive allele
Not eating enough protein
A dominant allele
questions.hint: One copy of the allele is enough to cause it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Polydactyly is inherited, not caught.
B: Incorrect — Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele.
C: Incorrect — Polydactyly is inherited. Diet doesn't cause it.
D: Correct — Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two parents without cystic fibrosis have a child with it. How is this possible?
options: The child caught it from another child
Both parents are carriers with one recessive allele each
Only one parent passed on the allele
One parent must have cystic fibrosis
questions.hint: You can carry an allele without showing it.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cystic fibrosis is inherited, not infectious.
B: Correct — Each parent passed one recessive allele to the child, who has two copies.
C: Incorrect — The child needs two recessive alleles, one from each parent.
D: Incorrect — Neither parent has it, but both carry the allele.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of which part of the cell?
options: Cell membranes
Chloroplasts
The cell wall
The nucleus
questions.hint: It is the part that controls what goes in and out.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes.
B: Incorrect — Human cells don't have chloroplasts.
C: Incorrect — Human cells don't have a cell wall.
D: Incorrect — Cystic fibrosis isn't a disorder of the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which is an ethical concern some people have about embryo screening?
options: Screening uses meiosis
Embryos with the disorder may be destroyed
Screening is expensive
Screening finds too few disorders
questions.hint: Ethics is about what is right or wrong, not about cost.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Screening tests embryos for alleles. It doesn't use meiosis.
B: Correct — Some people believe it is wrong to destroy embryos. This is an ethical issue.
C: Incorrect — Cost is an economic issue, not an ethical one.
D: Incorrect — This is about how well it works, not ethics.

questions.stem: How many pairs of chromosomes are in an ordinary human body cell?
options: 23 pairs
46 pairs
12 pairs
22 pairs
questions.hint: A human gamete has half this many single chromosomes.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Body cells contain 23 pairs: 46 chromosomes in total.
B: Incorrect — There are 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs.
C: Incorrect — Humans have more chromosomes than this.
D: Incorrect — 22 pairs control characteristics only, but there is also one pair of sex chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which sex chromosomes does a human male have?
options: X only
YY
XX
XY
questions.hint: In males the two sex chromosomes are different.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Males have two sex chromosomes, X and Y.
B: Incorrect — No human has two Y chromosomes and no X.
C: Incorrect — Females have two X chromosomes.
D: Correct — Males have one X and one Y chromosome.

questions.stem: What is the probability that a baby will be a boy?
questions.hint: Cross XX with XY.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Two of the four outcomes are XY, not one.
B: Incorrect — Only two of the four outcomes are XY.
C: Correct — The cross gives XX, XX, XY, XY: 2 out of 4 are XY.
D: Incorrect — Half of babies are expected to be girls.

questions.stem: Why does the father's gamete decide whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
options: Eggs carry either X or Y
All sperm carry Y
The father gives more chromosomes than the mother
All eggs carry X, but sperm carry either X or Y
questions.hint: Compare the sex chromosomes in eggs and in sperm.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Eggs always carry X, because the mother is XX.
B: Incorrect — Half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.
C: Incorrect — Each parent gives 23 chromosomes.
D: Correct — The egg always gives an X, so whether the baby is XX or XY depends on the sperm.

questions.stem: Differences between individuals in a population are called variation. What can cause variation?
options: Genes only
Genes, the environment, or both together
The environment only
Neither genes nor the environment
questions.hint: Think about nature and nurture.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The environment, such as diet, also causes variation.
B: Correct — Variation may be genetic, environmental or a combination of the two.
C: Incorrect — Inherited genes also cause variation.
D: Incorrect — Variation always has a cause: genes, environment or both.

questions.stem: Which of these is caused only by the environment?
options: Blood group
A scar from an accident
Having polydactyly
Natural eye colour
questions.hint: Which one did you not inherit from your parents?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Blood group is controlled by genes.
B: Correct — A scar comes from an injury, not from genes.
C: Incorrect — Polydactyly is caused by an inherited allele.
D: Incorrect — Eye colour is mainly inherited.

questions.stem: Where do all genetic variants come from?
options: Exercise
Mutations
Selective breeding
Diet
questions.hint: They are changes in the DNA.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Exercise changes the body, not the DNA passed on.
B: Correct — All variants arise from mutations.
C: Incorrect — Selective breeding chooses existing variants. It doesn't create them.
D: Incorrect — Diet causes environmental variation, not new alleles.

questions.stem: What effect do most mutations have on the phenotype?
options: They always give a new useful feature
They always change the number of chromosomes
They always cause disease
No effect
questions.hint: Mutations happen all the time, yet most people don't notice them.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A useful new phenotype is very rare.
B: Incorrect — Mutations usually change the DNA sequence, not the chromosome number.
C: Incorrect — Very few mutations cause disease.
D: Correct — Most mutations have no effect, some influence the phenotype, and very few decide it.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same genes. One twin grows up to be heavier than the other. What is the best explanation?
options: A difference in their inherited alleles
One twin has more chromosomes
Environmental factors, such as diet and exercise
Natural selection within one lifetime
questions.hint: If the genes are the same, what else is different?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Identical twins inherit the same alleles.
B: Incorrect — Both twins have the same number of chromosomes.
C: Correct — Identical genes mean any difference must come from the environment.
D: Incorrect — Natural selection acts on populations over many generations.

questions.stem: Very rarely, a mutation produces a new phenotype that suits a change in the environment. What can happen?
options: It can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species
The species becomes extinct straight away
Nothing, because mutations are never passed on
Every individual gets the same mutation at once
questions.hint: Individuals with this phenotype are more likely to survive and breed.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — The new phenotype is favoured and spreads through the population.
B: Incorrect — A helpful phenotype makes survival more likely, not less.
C: Incorrect — Mutations in gametes can be passed to offspring.
D: Incorrect — Mutations happen randomly in individuals. They spread through breeding.

questions.stem: What is evolution?
options: Moving a gene from one species to another
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time, through natural selection
A change in one animal during its lifetime
Humans choosing which animals breed
questions.hint: It happens to a population, over a long time.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is genetic engineering.
B: Correct — Evolution may result in the formation of a new species.
C: Incorrect — Changes during one lifetime aren't usually inherited.
D: Incorrect — That is selective breeding.

questions.stem: According to the theory of evolution, when did the first simple life forms develop?
options: About 10,000 years ago
About 1 million years ago
More than three billion years ago
About 200 years ago
questions.hint: It is a very, very long time ago.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That is roughly when humans began farming.
B: Incorrect — Life began far earlier than this.
C: Correct — All species have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
D: Incorrect — That is around when Darwin lived.

questions.stem: Two populations of one species become very different. When have they become two separate species?
options: When they look slightly different
When they eat different food
When they live in different countries
When they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.hint: Think about their offspring.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Individuals in one species often look different.
B: Incorrect — Different diets don't make them separate species.
C: Incorrect — Living apart alone doesn't make them separate species.
D: Correct — This is how new species form.

questions.stem: Some rabbits in a cold area have thicker fur than others because of a mutation. Which explains why, over many generations, most of the rabbits end up with thick fur?
options: Rabbits choose to grow thicker fur
Thin-furred rabbits turn into thick-furred rabbits
Thick-furred rabbits are more likely to survive and breed, passing on the allele
The cold makes each rabbit grow thicker fur, which it then passes on
questions.hint: Survive → breed → pass on.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Organisms can't choose their alleles.
B: Incorrect — Individuals don't evolve. Populations change over generations.
C: Correct — Natural selection favours the variant best suited to the environment.
D: Incorrect — Changes during a lifetime aren't inherited. That is Lamarck's idea.

questions.stem: What is selective breeding?
options: Humans choosing which plants or animals breed, to get a characteristic they want
Making an exact copy of an adult animal
Animals choosing their own mates in the wild
Putting a gene from one organism into another
questions.hint: It is also called artificial selection.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics.
B: Incorrect — That is cloning.
C: Incorrect — That is part of natural selection.
D: Incorrect — That is genetic engineering.

questions.stem: A farmer wants cows that make more milk. Which method uses selective breeding?
options: Breed the cows that give most milk, then keep breeding the best offspring for many generations
Give all the cows more food
Breed cows at random and hope for the best
Breed the best cows once, then stop
questions.hint: It takes many generations.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Parents with the desired characteristic are bred, and this repeats until all offspring show it.
B: Incorrect — More food changes the cows, not their genes.
C: Incorrect — Selective breeding means choosing the parents.
D: Incorrect — One generation isn't enough. It continues over many generations.

questions.stem: What is a risk of selective breeding?
options: It always produces sterile offspring
It puts genes from other species into food
Inbreeding can make some breeds prone to disease or inherited defects
It makes animals grow too fast to survive
questions.hint: The animals bred together are often closely related.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Selectively bred animals can usually breed.
B: Incorrect — That is a concern about genetic engineering.
C: Correct — Breeding close relatives reduces variation and makes harmful alleles more likely to show.
D: Incorrect — This isn't the main risk named in the spec.

questions.stem: Which of these is a characteristic that crops are often selectively bred for?
options: Being more likely to catch disease
Resistance to disease
Smaller harvests
Fewer seeds that can grow
questions.hint: Farmers want fewer crops to die.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Farmers want the opposite.
B: Correct — Disease-resistant crops give more food.
C: Incorrect — Farmers want bigger harvests.
D: Incorrect — Farmers want more crops, not fewer.

questions.stem: What is genetic engineering?
options: Changing an organism's genome by adding a gene from another organism
Changing an organism's diet to make it grow bigger
Choosing parents with good features and breeding them
Making identical copies of a plant from cuttings
questions.hint: It involves two different organisms.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This gives the organism a desired characteristic.
B: Incorrect — That is an environmental change, not a genetic one.
C: Incorrect — That is selective breeding.
D: Incorrect — That is cloning.

questions.stem: Bacteria have been genetically engineered to make which useful substance for people with diabetes?
options: Human insulin
Adrenaline
Antibiotics
Glucagon
questions.hint: It is a hormone that lowers blood glucose.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Bacteria with the human insulin gene make insulin to treat diabetes.
B: Incorrect — Adrenaline isn't used to treat diabetes.
C: Incorrect — Antibiotics come from fungi and bacteria naturally.
D: Incorrect — Glucagon raises blood glucose. It isn't the example in the spec.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of GM crops?
options: They have no effect on wild flowers or insects
They never need water
Everyone agrees they are completely safe to eat
They can be resistant to insect attack, so yields are higher
questions.hint: Farmers lose less of their crop.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The effect on wild flowers and insects is a concern.
B: Incorrect — GM crops still need water.
C: Incorrect — Some people feel the effects on health haven't been fully explored.
D: Correct — GM crops can resist insects or herbicides and generally give increased yields.

questions.stem: Which is a concern some people have about GM crops?
options: They give lower yields
They can't be grown in fields
They are not resistant to anything
They may affect populations of wild flowers and insects
questions.hint: Think about the wildlife living around the fields.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — GM crops generally give higher yields.
B: Incorrect — GM crops are grown in fields.
C: Incorrect — Many GM crops are resistant to insects or herbicides.
D: Correct — This is a concern, along with the unknown long-term effects on human health.

questions.stem: In genetic engineering, what is used to cut out the required gene?
options: Antibiotics
An electric shock
Enzymes
A virus
questions.hint: They are biological catalysts.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibiotics kill bacteria. They don't cut DNA.
B: Incorrect — An electric shock is used in adult cell cloning.
C: Correct — Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene.
D: Incorrect — A virus can be used as a vector to carry the gene, not to cut it out.

questions.stem: In genetic engineering, what is a vector?
options: A type of gamete
Something that carries the gene into the cell, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus
The organism the gene came from
An enzyme that cuts DNA
questions.hint: It carries the gene into the new cell.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A vector isn't a sex cell.
B: Correct — The gene is inserted into the vector, which then inserts it into the required cells.
C: Incorrect — That is the donor organism.
D: Incorrect — Enzymes cut out the gene. The vector carries it.

questions.stem: Why are genes transferred to animal or plant cells at an early stage of development?
options: Because early cells are bigger
So that the gene is removed again later
So the organism develops with the desired characteristic in all its cells
Because adult cells have no DNA
questions.hint: Think about how many cells end up with the new gene.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Size isn't the reason.
B: Incorrect — The aim is to keep the gene.
C: Correct — Cells copied from the early cells all carry the gene.
D: Incorrect — Adult cells do have DNA.

questions.stem: Why might genetic engineering help people with inherited disorders in the future?
options: It turns recessive alleles into dominant ones
It is already used to cure every inherited disorder
It might be used to correct or replace a faulty allele
It can stop all mutations from happening
questions.hint: Inherited disorders are caused by alleles.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That isn't how genetic engineering works.
B: Incorrect — This is still being researched.
C: Correct — Medical research is exploring genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.
D: Incorrect — Mutations happen continuously.

questions.stem: A gardener takes cuttings from a parent plant. What will the new plants be like?
options: Unable to grow
Genetically identical to the parent
Half like the parent and half like another plant
Genetically different from the parent
questions.hint: Cuttings are a type of asexual reproduction.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Cuttings grow into new plants.
B: Correct — Cuttings produce many identical new plants (clones).
C: Incorrect — Only one parent is involved.
D: Incorrect — There is no mixing of genetic information.

questions.stem: Why is tissue culture useful?
options: It can preserve rare plant species and grow many identical plants for nurseries
It creates brand new species
It is used to clone adult animals
It produces lots of variation
questions.hint: It uses small groups of cells from a plant.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Tissue culture grows identical plants from a few cells.
B: Incorrect — The plants are identical to the parent.
C: Incorrect — Tissue culture is used for plants.
D: Incorrect — Tissue culture produces clones.

questions.stem: What happens in an embryo transplant?
options: Cells are split apart from a developing animal embryo and the identical embryos are put into host mothers
A piece of a plant stem is planted
The nucleus of a skin cell is put into an egg cell
A gene is added to an embryo
questions.hint: It happens before the cells become specialised.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This makes several identical animals.
B: Incorrect — That is a cutting.
C: Incorrect — That is adult cell cloning.
D: Incorrect — That is genetic engineering.

questions.stem: In adult cell cloning, what is the correct order of steps?
options: Insert an adult nucleus into an egg that keeps its own nucleus → put it into a womb
Remove the nucleus from an egg → insert a nucleus from an adult body cell → give an electric shock → put the embryo into a womb
Fertilise an egg with sperm → split the embryo → put the embryos into host mothers
Give an electric shock → remove the nucleus from an egg → put the embryo into a womb → insert an adult nucleus
questions.hint: The egg has to lose its own nucleus first.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The egg's own nucleus is removed first.
B: Correct — This is the order given in the spec.
C: Incorrect — That describes embryo transplants.
D: Incorrect — The nucleus must be swapped before the shock.

questions.stem: A skin cell nucleus from sheep A is put into an empty egg cell from sheep B. The embryo grows in sheep C. Which sheep is the lamb genetically identical to?
options: Sheep C
Sheep A
A mix of sheep A and B
Sheep B
questions.hint: Where did the nucleus come from?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Sheep C only carries the embryo.
B: Correct — The embryo has the same genetic information as the adult skin cell.
C: Incorrect — No gametes join, so there is no mixing.
D: Incorrect — Sheep B's egg had its nucleus removed.

questions.stem: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection after a round-the-world expedition?
options: Gregor Mendel
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Charles Darwin
Carl Linnaeus
questions.hint: He wrote On the Origin of Species.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Mendel studied inheritance in plants.
B: Incorrect — Lamarck had a different theory, that changes in a lifetime are inherited.
C: Correct — Darwin's observations, years of experiments and knowledge of fossils led to his theory.
D: Incorrect — Linnaeus developed the classification system.

questions.stem: In which year did Darwin publish On the Origin of Species?
questions.hint: It was in the mid-19th century.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — By then, the structure of DNA had already been worked out.
B: Incorrect — This is the year Darwin was born, not when he published.
C: Incorrect — This is a century too early.
D: Correct — Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

questions.stem: Which was a reason Darwin's theory was only gradually accepted?
options: Everyone already believed in natural selection
DNA had already shown the theory was wrong
The way inheritance and variation worked wasn't known until 50 years later
Darwin had made no observations
questions.hint: People didn't yet know how features were passed on.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — The ideas were new and controversial.
B: Incorrect — DNA was worked out much later, and it supports the theory.
C: Correct — Without knowing about genes, the theory was harder to accept.
D: Incorrect — Darwin made many observations on his expedition.

questions.stem: What was Lamarck's theory mainly based on?
options: Units of inheritance passed on unchanged
Natural selection of variants best suited to the environment
Organisms are grouped into three domains
Changes that happen to an organism during its lifetime can be inherited
questions.hint: Think of a giraffe stretching its neck.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — That was Mendel's idea.
B: Incorrect — That is Darwin's theory.
C: Incorrect — That was Woese's system.
D: Correct — We now know this type of inheritance can't happen in the vast majority of cases.

questions.stem: How would Darwin explain why giraffes have long necks?
options: Giraffes with longer necks reached more food, survived to breed, and passed on the characteristic
A gene from another animal was added to giraffes
Giraffes chose to grow longer necks
Giraffes stretched their necks, and their young were born with longer necks
questions.hint: Darwin's idea starts with variation that already exists.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Individuals best suited to the environment survive and pass on their characteristics.
B: Incorrect — That is genetic engineering.
C: Incorrect — Organisms can't choose their characteristics.
D: Incorrect — This is Lamarck's idea.

questions.stem: What is Alfred Russel Wallace best known for?
options: Work on warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation
Discovering the structure of DNA
The three-domain system
Breeding experiments on plants
questions.hint: He came up with natural selection at the same time as Darwin.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Wallace independently proposed natural selection and published joint writings with Darwin in 1858.
B: Incorrect — DNA's structure was worked out in the mid-20th century.
C: Incorrect — That was Carl Woese.
D: Incorrect — That was Mendel.

questions.stem: What prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species in 1859?
options: Lamarck's theory was proved correct
The structure of DNA was discovered
Mendel asked him to
Joint writings with Wallace were published the year before
questions.hint: Someone else had the same idea.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Lamarck's theory wasn't proved correct.
B: Incorrect — That happened in the mid-20th century.
C: Incorrect — Mendel's work wasn't widely known at the time.
D: Correct — Wallace's joint writings with Darwin in 1858 prompted Darwin to publish.

questions.stem: A population of birds is split in two by a new mountain range. Which explains how a new species could form?
options: The birds decide to become two species
The mountain causes the same mutation in every bird
The two groups stay exactly the same forever
Each group adapts to its own conditions by natural selection until they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.hint: Isolation → different conditions → natural selection → ...
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Species don't choose to change.
B: Incorrect — Mutations are random and happen in individuals.
C: Incorrect — Different conditions lead to natural selection of different variants.
D: Correct — Isolated populations change separately until they become different species.

questions.stem: In the mid-19th century, who carried out breeding experiments on plants and found that characteristics are passed on as "units"?
options: Gregor Mendel
Carl Woese
Charles Darwin
Alfred Russel Wallace
questions.hint: He is often called the father of genetics.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Mendel found that each characteristic is determined by units passed on unchanged.
B: Incorrect — Woese proposed the three-domain system.
C: Incorrect — Darwin proposed natural selection.
D: Incorrect — Wallace worked on speciation and warning colouration.

questions.stem: What do we now call Mendel's "units"?
options: Species
Genes
Gametes
Cells
questions.hint: They are found on chromosomes.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A species is a group of organisms.
B: Correct — In the early 20th century, scientists realised that Mendel's units were genes on chromosomes.
C: Incorrect — Gametes carry the units but aren't the units themselves.
D: Incorrect — Cells are much bigger than units of inheritance.

questions.stem: Why wasn't the importance of Mendel's work recognised until after his death?
options: He worked with animals that nobody had heard of
His results were proved to be wrong
DNA had already explained everything
Chromosomes and genes weren't known about, so nobody could explain his "units"
questions.hint: What hadn't been discovered yet?
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Mendel worked with plants.
B: Incorrect — His results were correct.
C: Incorrect — DNA's structure was worked out in the mid-20th century, long after Mendel.
D: Correct — Only later did scientists see that chromosomes behave like Mendel's units.

questions.stem: Which shows the correct order of discoveries in genetics?
options: Structure of DNA → Mendel's units → chromosomes seen
Chromosomes linked to units → Mendel's units → structure of DNA
Mendel's units → chromosomes seen in dividing cells → units linked to chromosomes → structure of DNA
Structure of DNA → chromosomes seen → Mendel's units
questions.hint: Start in the mid-19th century and finish in the mid-20th.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — DNA's structure was worked out last.
B: Incorrect — Mendel's work came before chromosomes were linked to units.
C: Correct — This work by many scientists led to gene theory.
D: Incorrect — This is backwards.

questions.stem: Which of these is evidence for evolution?
options: Photosynthesis and respiration
Fossils and antibiotic resistance in bacteria
Vaccines and painkillers
Selective breeding and cloning
questions.hint: One is found in rocks, the other in hospitals.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are life processes.
B: Correct — Both show how organisms change over time.
C: Incorrect — These are medicines.
D: Incorrect — These are human techniques, not evidence for natural evolution.

questions.stem: What are fossils?
options: Rocks shaped to look like animals
Bones of animals that died last year
The remains of organisms from millions of years ago
Living organisms that never change
questions.hint: They are found in rocks.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Fossils come from real organisms.
B: Incorrect — Fossils are millions of years old.
C: Correct — Fossils are found in rocks.
D: Incorrect — Fossils are remains, not living things.

questions.stem: Which is one way a fossil can form?
options: An organism is frozen for a few days
Bacteria turn the organism into new cells
Parts of an organism don't decay because the conditions for decay are absent
An organism decays completely and leaves nothing
questions.hint: Decay needs certain conditions.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — A few days isn't long enough to make a fossil.
B: Incorrect — That isn't how fossils form.
C: Correct — Fossils also form when parts are replaced by minerals, or as preserved traces.
D: Incorrect — Then there would be nothing to fossilise.

questions.stem: Which of these is a trace fossil?
options: An insect trapped in amber
A footprint preserved in rock
A bone replaced by minerals
A living fern
questions.hint: It shows where an organism has been, not the organism itself.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — This is the organism itself, preserved because decay couldn't happen.
B: Correct — Footprints, burrows and rootlet traces are preserved traces.
C: Incorrect — This is a fossil of part of the organism, not a trace.
D: Incorrect — A living plant isn't a fossil.

questions.stem: Why can't scientists be certain about how life began on Earth?
options: There are no fossils at all
Fossils can't show how organisms have changed
Early life forms were too large to fossilise
Early life was soft-bodied and left few traces, and most were destroyed by geological activity
questions.hint: Think about what early life forms were like.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — There are many fossils, but the early record is incomplete.
B: Incorrect — Fossils do show how much organisms have changed.
C: Incorrect — Early life forms were small and soft-bodied.
D: Correct — So the fossil record is incomplete.

questions.stem: When is a species extinct?
options: When there are no individuals of the species still alive
When it moves to a new habitat
When it is only found in zoos
When numbers fall by half
questions.hint: Think about how many are left.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Extinction is when no individuals remain.
B: Incorrect — Moving doesn't make it extinct.
C: Incorrect — Animals in zoos are still alive.
D: Incorrect — The species still exists.

questions.stem: Which factor could contribute to a species becoming extinct?
options: A new predator arriving in its habitat
Plenty of food
Lots of genetic variation
Fewer competitors
questions.hint: Think about something that kills many individuals.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — New predators, new diseases, habitat loss and climate change can all cause extinction.
B: Incorrect — More food helps a species survive.
C: Incorrect — Variation makes survival more likely.
D: Incorrect — Less competition helps a species survive.

questions.stem: What is MRSA?
options: A new antibiotic
A type of vaccine
A virus that causes flu
A bacterium that is resistant to antibiotics
questions.hint: It is a well-known hospital "superbug".
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — MRSA is the bacterium, not a treatment.
B: Incorrect — MRSA isn't a vaccine.
C: Incorrect — MRSA is a bacterium, not a virus.
D: Correct — MRSA is a strain of bacteria that antibiotics don't kill.

questions.stem: Why can bacteria evolve rapidly?
options: They reproduce sexually
They reproduce at a fast rate
They have no DNA
They choose to change
questions.hint: Think about how often new generations appear.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bacteria reproduce asexually.
B: Correct — Many generations in a short time means natural selection works quickly.
C: Incorrect — Bacteria do have DNA.
D: Incorrect — Bacteria can't choose to evolve.

questions.stem: How does a population of antibiotic-resistant bacteria build up?
options: The antibiotic teaches the bacteria to resist it
All the bacteria mutate at the same time in the same way
The patient's white blood cells make the bacteria resistant
A mutation makes some bacteria resistant; they survive the antibiotic and reproduce, so the resistant strain rises
questions.hint: Mutation → survival → reproduction.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bacteria don't learn. Resistance comes from random mutations.
B: Incorrect — Mutations are random, in individual bacteria.
C: Incorrect — White blood cells destroy pathogens. They don't cause resistance.
D: Correct — The resistant strain then spreads because people aren't immune and there is no effective treatment.

questions.stem: Why should patients complete their course of antibiotics?
options: So their immune system stops working
Because antibiotics also kill viruses
So that they become immune to the antibiotic
So all the bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate into resistant strains
questions.hint: Think about the bacteria left behind.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Antibiotics don't affect the immune system like this.
B: Incorrect — Antibiotics don't kill viruses.
C: Incorrect — People don't become immune to antibiotics. Bacteria become resistant.
D: Correct — Stopping early can leave bacteria alive that may form resistant strains.

questions.stem: Which action helps reduce the rate at which antibiotic-resistant strains develop?
options: Using antibiotics as often as possible
Restricting the use of antibiotics in farming
Stopping antibiotics as soon as you feel better
Prescribing antibiotics for colds and flu
questions.hint: Use antibiotics only when they are really needed.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — More use gives more chances for resistance to develop.
B: Correct — Restricting agricultural use, and not prescribing for viral or non-serious infections, both help.
C: Incorrect — This can leave bacteria alive.
D: Incorrect — Colds and flu are viral, so antibiotics don't help and resistance is more likely.

questions.stem: Why are scientists worried about relying on new antibiotics to fight resistant bacteria?
options: Bacteria can't become resistant to new antibiotics
New antibiotics are costly and slow to develop, so they are unlikely to keep up with new resistant strains
New antibiotics are made very quickly and cheaply
New antibiotics also kill viruses
questions.hint: Think about time and cost.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Bacteria can become resistant to any antibiotic.
B: Correct — Resistant strains can appear faster than new antibiotics are made.
C: Incorrect — Development is costly and slow.
D: Incorrect — Antibiotics don't kill viruses.

questions.stem: Who developed the traditional system for classifying living things by their structure and characteristics?
options: Carl Woese
Carl Linnaeus
Charles Darwin
Gregor Mendel
questions.hint: His system gives every organism a two-part name.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Woese developed the three-domain system using chemical analysis.
B: Correct — Linnaeus classified living things from kingdom down to species.
C: Incorrect — Darwin proposed natural selection.
D: Incorrect — Mendel studied inheritance.

questions.stem: Which shows the Linnaean groups in order, from largest to smallest?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, order, phylum, class, family, species, genus
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
Kingdom, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
questions.hint: It starts with kingdom and ends with species.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — This is the correct order.
B: Incorrect — Genus comes before species.
C: Incorrect — This is smallest to largest.
D: Incorrect — Phylum comes before class, and family before genus.

questions.stem: In the binomial system, which two parts make up an organism's name?
options: Class and order
Genus and species
Kingdom and phylum
Family and genus
questions.hint: "Bi" means two. They are the two smallest groups.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These aren't used in the two-part name.
B: Correct — For example, Homo sapiens: Homo is the genus and sapiens the species.
C: Incorrect — These are the largest groups.
D: Incorrect — The name is genus then species.

questions.stem: The lion's scientific name is Panthera leo. What is its genus?
options: leo
Animal
Cat family
Panthera
questions.hint: The genus comes first.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — leo is the species name.
B: Incorrect — Animals is a kingdom.
C: Incorrect — Family is a larger group than genus.
D: Correct — In the binomial system the genus comes first.

questions.stem: Lions and tigers are both in the genus Panthera. Which must also be true?
options: They are in the same family
They can breed to produce fertile offspring
They are in different orders
They are the same species
questions.hint: Each genus sits inside one family.
questions.rationale:
A: Correct — Organisms in the same genus also share all the larger groups above it.
B: Incorrect — Different species usually can't produce fertile offspring.
C: Incorrect — Being in one genus means they share an order.
D: Incorrect — They share a genus but are different species.

questions.stem: Who developed the three-domain system?
options: Carl Linnaeus
Charles Darwin
Alfred Russel Wallace
Carl Woese
questions.hint: His system came from chemical analysis.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Linnaeus developed the older system based on structure.
B: Incorrect — Darwin proposed natural selection.
C: Incorrect — Wallace worked on speciation.
D: Correct — Woese used evidence from chemical analysis.

questions.stem: Which are the three domains?
options: Kingdom, genus and species
Viruses, bacteria and fungi
Archaea, bacteria and eukaryota
Plants, animals and fungi
questions.hint: One of them includes all plants and animals.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are Linnaean groups.
B: Incorrect — Viruses aren't one of the three domains.
C: Correct — Organisms are divided into these three domains.
D: Incorrect — These are all in one domain: eukaryota.

questions.stem: Which domain do fungi belong to?
options: Plantae
Bacteria
Archaea
Eukaryota
questions.hint: Fungi cells have a nucleus.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Plantae isn't one of the three domains.
B: Incorrect — Bacteria are true bacteria.
C: Incorrect — Archaea are primitive bacteria, often in extreme environments.
D: Correct — Eukaryota includes protists, fungi, plants and animals.

questions.stem: Which organisms are in the domain archaea?
options: Plants and animals
True bacteria
Primitive bacteria, usually living in extreme environments
Fungi
questions.hint: They often live in very hot or very salty places.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — These are eukaryota.
B: Incorrect — These are in the domain bacteria.
C: Correct — Archaea are primitive bacteria that often live in extreme places.
D: Incorrect — Fungi are eukaryota.

questions.stem: Why have new models of classification been proposed since Linnaeus?
options: All organisms have stopped evolving
Better microscopes showed internal structures, and chemical analysis gave new evidence
Linnaeus's system had no groups
Scientists now classify only by colour
questions.hint: Think about new tools scientists have.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Organisms continue to evolve.
B: Correct — Developments in biology changed how organisms are grouped.
C: Incorrect — Linnaeus's system had seven levels of groups.
D: Incorrect — Classification uses structure and chemical evidence, not just colour.

questions.stem: What information do scientists use to build evolutionary trees?
options: Only data about where organisms live
Only the size of each organism
Classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct ones
Only the date each species was named
questions.hint: They include both living and extinct organisms.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Location alone doesn't show relationships.
B: Incorrect — Size alone doesn't show relationships.
C: Correct — Evolutionary trees show how scientists believe organisms are related.
D: Incorrect — When a species was named doesn't show relationships.

questions.stem: An evolutionary tree shows that species P and Q split from a common ancestor 5 million years ago. Species R split from their line 30 million years ago. Which two species are most closely related?
options: Q and R
They are all equally related
P and R
P and Q
questions.hint: The more recent the common ancestor, the closer the relationship.
questions.rationale:
A: Incorrect — Q and R last shared an ancestor 30 million years ago.
B: Incorrect — P and Q split much more recently than R.
C: Incorrect — P and R last shared an ancestor 30 million years ago.
D: Correct — P and Q share the most recent common ancestor.
